title: Part 1, Chapter 34
paragraphs: Continuing the novel of "The Ill-Advised Curiosity"

"They say an army looks wrong without its general and a castle without its castellan, and I'd add that a young married woman looks worse still without her husband — unless there are very good reasons for it. I feel so out of sorts without you, and so unable to bear this separation, that if you don't come back soon I'll have to go take refuge at my parents' house, even if it means leaving yours unguarded; for the guardian you left me — if he deserved that title at all — has, I suspect, more regard for his own pleasure than for anything that concerns you. You're a perceptive man; I don't need to say more, nor would it be proper for me to say more."

Anselmo received this letter and gathered from it that Lothario had already begun his task and that Camilla must have answered him exactly as he had hoped. Delighted beyond measure at the news, he sent word back to her not to leave the house on any account, since he would be returning very shortly. Camilla was astonished at Anselmo's reply, which left her in a worse bind than before, for she dared neither stay in her own house nor go to her parents'; staying put her virtue in danger, and leaving meant disobeying her husband. In the end she chose the worse course for herself — to remain — resolving not to flee Lothario's presence so as not to give her servants something to gossip about. She now regretted writing as she had to her husband, afraid he might imagine that Lothario had sensed in her some lightness that had encouraged him to drop the respect he owed her; but trusting her own rectitude she put her faith in God and her virtuous intentions, with which she hoped to resist Lothario's pursuits in silence and say nothing to her husband so as not to drag him into any quarrel or trouble. She even began to think how she might excuse Lothario to Anselmo when he asked what had made her write that letter. With these resolutions — more honourable than wise or effective — she sat through the next day listening to Lothario, who pressed his suit so hard that Camilla's firmness began to waver, and her virtue had its hands full keeping her eyes from betraying a certain tender pity that Lothario's tears and pleas had stirred in her heart. Lothario noticed all this, and it inflamed him further. In short, he felt that while Anselmo's absence gave him time and opportunity he had to press the siege of the fortress, so he attacked her self-esteem with praises of her beauty — for nothing levels the castle-walls of a fair woman's vanity faster than vanity itself on the tongue of flattery. With the most relentless persistence he undermined the rock of her purity with such engines that, had Camilla been bronze, she would still have fallen. He wept, he begged, he promised, he flattered, he pestered, he feigned with such feeling and apparent sincerity that he overthrew Camilla's virtuous resolves and won the triumph he least expected and most longed for. Camilla yielded; Camilla fell. But what wonder, if Lothario's own friendship could not stand firm? A clear proof to us that the passion of love is to be conquered only by fleeing from it, and that no one should engage in a struggle with so mighty an enemy; for divine strength is needed to defeat its human power. Only Leonela knew of her mistress's weakness, since the two false friends and new lovers could not hide it from her. Lothario did not tell Camilla what Anselmo's plan had been, nor that Anselmo himself had given him the opportunity to achieve such an outcome, for fear she would undervalue his love and think that he had courted her by accident and reluctantly, not of his own choice.

A few days later Anselmo returned home and did not see what had been lost — what he had so casually risked and so highly prized. He went at once to see Lothario, and found him in. They embraced, and Anselmo asked for the news of his life or his death.

"The news I have to give you, Anselmo my friend," said Lothario, "is that you possess a wife fit to be the model and crown of all good wives. The words I directed at her were swept away on the wind; my promises were despised; my presents were refused; the fake tears I shed were openly mocked. In short, just as Camilla is the essence of all beauty, she is the treasure-house of purity, and gentleness and modesty live in her along with every virtue that can bring a woman praise, honour, and happiness. Take back your money, my friend; here it is, and I never had to touch it, for Camilla's chastity does not bow to anything as cheap as gifts or promises. Be satisfied, Anselmo, and don't go testing her any further; you have crossed dryshod through the sea of those doubts and suspicions men commonly entertain about women — don't plunge again into the deep ocean of fresh embarrassments, or, with another pilot, test the soundness of the boat that Heaven has granted you for your passage across this life. Count yourself safe in port, moor yourself with the anchor of sound reflection, and rest in peace until you are summoned to pay that debt no nobility on earth can escape paying."

Anselmo was completely satisfied by Lothario's words and believed them as fully as if they had been spoken by an oracle; nevertheless, he begged him not to give the project up, if only for curiosity and amusement — though from now on he need not press as hard as before. All he wanted was for Lothario to write some verses praising her under the name of Chloris, for he himself would let her think Lothario was in love with a lady to whom he had given that name so that he could sing her praises with the decorum her modesty deserved; and if Lothario didn't want the trouble of writing the verses, he would compose them himself.

"That won't be necessary," said Lothario, "for the muses are not so hostile to me but that they visit me now and then in the course of a year. Tell Camilla what you propose about this pretended love of mine; as for the verses, I'll make them, and if they aren't as good as the subject deserves they will at least be the best I can produce." An agreement to this effect was reached between the friends — the ill-advised one and the treacherous one — and Anselmo, going home, asked Camilla the question she was already surprised he had not asked: what had made her write the letter she had sent him. Camilla replied that it had seemed to her Lothario looked at her somewhat more freely than when Anselmo had been at home, but that she was now undeceived and believed it had only been her own imagination, since Lothario now avoided seeing her or being alone with her. Anselmo told her she could be quite easy about that suspicion, because he knew Lothario was in love with a young lady of rank in the city whom he was celebrating under the name of Chloris, and that even if he were not, his loyalty and their great friendship left no room for fear. Had Camilla not already been warned by Lothario that this love for Chloris was a pretence — and that he had told Anselmo about it so as to be able sometimes to give voice to praise of Camilla herself — she would no doubt have fallen into the despairing toils of jealousy; but being forewarned she took the startling news without distress.

The next day, as the three of them were at table, Anselmo asked Lothario to recite something of what he had composed for his mistress Chloris; since Camilla did not know her, he could say whatever he liked.

"Even if she knew her," Lothario replied, "I would hide nothing, for when a lover praises his lady's beauty and accuses her of cruelty, he casts no slur upon her good name; in any case, all I can say is that yesterday I made a sonnet on the ingratitude of this Chloris, and it goes like this:
SONNET

At midnight, in the silence, when the eyes Of happier mortals balmy slumbers close, The weary tale of my unnumbered woes To Chloris and to Heaven is wont to rise. And when the light of day returning dyes The portals of the east with tints of rose, With undiminished force my sorrow flows In broken accents and in burning sighs. And when the sun ascends his star-girt throne, And on the earth pours down his midday beams, Noon but renews my wailing and my tears; And with the night again goes up my moan. Yet ever in my agony it seems To me that neither Heaven nor Chloris hears."

The sonnet pleased Camilla, and pleased Anselmo even more — he praised it and said the lady was excessively cruel to give no return for such manifest sincerity. At which Camilla asked, "Then everything love-stricken poets say is true?"
"As poets, they don't tell the truth," replied Lothario; "but as lovers they are as truthful as they are inarticulate."

"No doubt about that," said Anselmo, eager to back up and reinforce Lothario's ideas with Camilla — who was as oblivious to his design as she was deep in love with Lothario. Taking pleasure in anything that was his, and knowing that his thoughts and writings were aimed at her, that she herself was the real Chloris, she asked him to recite some other sonnet or verses if he remembered any.
"I do," Lothario replied, "but I don't think it as good as the first — or, to put it more correctly, less bad; though you can easily judge for yourselves, since here it is.
SONNET

I know that I am doomed; death is to me As certain as that thou, ungrateful fair, Dead at thy feet shouldst see me lying, ere My heart repented of its love for thee. If buried in oblivion I should be, Bereft of life, fame, favour, even there It would be found that I thy image bear Deep graven in my breast for all to see. This like some holy relic do I prize To save me from the fate my truth entails, Truth that to thy hard heart its vigour owes. Alas for him that under lowering skies, In peril o'er a trackless ocean sails, Where neither friendly port nor pole-star shows."

Anselmo praised this second sonnet as he had praised the first, adding one more link to the chain he was binding around himself and locking in his own dishonour; for the more Lothario was working to disgrace him, the more Anselmo told him he was honouring him; and so each step Camilla descended toward the depths of her degradation, she seemed, in his eyes, to climb toward the summit of virtue and a spotless reputation.

It happened that, finding herself alone one day with her maid, Camilla said to her, "I'm ashamed when I think, my dear Leonela, how lightly I valued myself, that I didn't make Lothario buy at least with some expense of time the complete possession of me that I yielded so quickly of my own free will. I'm afraid he'll think badly of my pliancy or lightness, and forget the irresistible force he brought to bear on me."

"Don't let that worry you, my lady," said Leonela. "It doesn't lessen the value of a thing given, or make it less precious, that the gift came quickly — provided it really is valuable and worth prizing. In fact, they say that whoever gives quickly gives twice."
"They also say," Camilla replied, "that what costs little is valued less."

"That saying doesn't apply in your case," Leonela said. "For love, as I've heard tell, sometimes flies and sometimes walks; with one it runs, with another it crawls; some it cools, others it burns; some it wounds, others it kills; it sets out on the course of its desires and at the same moment completes and ends it; in the morning it lays siege to a fortress, and by night it has taken the place, since there's no power that can resist it. So what are you afraid of, what are you dreading, when the same thing must have happened to Lothario — love having picked my lord's absence as the instrument for subduing you? And it was absolutely necessary to finish then what love had decided on, without allowing time for Anselmo to come back and by his presence force the work to be left unfinished; for love has no better agent for carrying out its designs than opportunity, and it uses opportunity in everything it does, especially at the outset. I know all this well myself, more by experience than hearsay, and one day, señora, I'll enlighten you on the subject, for I'm flesh and blood like you. What's more, lady Camilla, you didn't surrender or yield so quickly without first seeing Lothario's whole soul in his eyes, in his sighs, in his words, his promises, and his gifts — and by all that, and by his good qualities, you saw how worthy he was of your love. That being the case, don't let these scrupulous, prudish ideas trouble your imagination; rest assured that Lothario prizes you as you do him, and be content and satisfied that, since you have been caught in love's noose, the one who caught you is of worth and merit — one who not only has the four S's that true lovers are said to need, but a whole alphabet. Just listen and you'll see how I can rattle it off: he is, to my eyes and mind, Amiable, Brave, Courteous, Distinguished, Elegant, Fond, Gay, Honourable, Illustrious, Loyal, Manly, Noble, Open, Polite, Quickwitted, Rich, and the S's according to the saying, and then Tender, Veracious; X doesn't suit him, since it's a harsh letter; Y has been given already; and Z, Zealous for your honour."

Camilla laughed at her maid's alphabet, and realised she was more experienced in love affairs than she had let on. Leonela admitted as much, confessing to Camilla that she had a love affair with a young man of good family in the same city. Camilla was uneasy at this, afraid it might end up endangering her own honour, and asked whether the affair had gone beyond words. With little shame and much brazenness Leonela said it had — for it is certain that a mistress's recklessness makes servants shameless: when they see their mistresses make a false step, they think nothing of going wrong themselves, or of being found out. All Camilla could do was beg Leonela to say nothing of her doings to the man she called her lover, and to conduct her own affairs in secret so they wouldn't reach the ears of Anselmo or Lothario. Leonela promised she would, but kept her word in a way that confirmed Camilla's fear of losing her reputation through her; for this depraved and bold Leonela, as soon as she noticed that her mistress's bearing was not what it had been, had the audacity to bring her lover into the house, confident that even if her mistress saw him she wouldn't dare expose him. This is one of the harms a mistress's sins bring with them: she makes herself the slave of her own servants and is forced to hide their loose conduct and depravities — as was the case with Camilla, who, though she saw not once but many times that Leonela was with her lover in some room of the house, not only didn't dare to scold her, but gave her opportunities to conceal him and removed all difficulties to keep him from being seen by her husband. She could not, however, prevent him from being seen one morning, slipping out at daybreak, by Lothario — who, not knowing who he was, at first took him for a ghost; but as soon as he saw him hurry off, muffling his face with his cloak and hiding himself with care and caution, he dismissed that foolish notion and adopted another, which would have been the ruin of everything if Camilla had not found a remedy. It did not occur to Lothario that this man he had seen leaving Anselmo's house at such an odd hour could have entered it on Leonela's account; he did not even remember that such a person as Leonela existed. All he thought was that, since Camilla had been light and yielding with him, she had been the same with someone else; for this further penalty an erring woman's sin brings with it: her honour is mistrusted even by the man to whose advances and persuasions she has yielded. He believes she has surrendered more easily to others, and gives full credit to every suspicion that enters his mind. All Lothario's good sense seemed to fail him at this point; all his prudent maxims slipped his memory; for without one rational reflection, and without more ado, in his impatience and the blindness of the jealous rage gnawing at his heart, dying to revenge himself on Camilla — who had done him no wrong — he hurried to Anselmo before he was up and said: "Anselmo, you should know that for several days now I have been wrestling with myself, trying to hold back what it is no longer possible or right for me to conceal from you. Camilla's fortress has surrendered, and is ready to submit to my will; and if I have been slow to reveal this to you, it was to see whether it might be some light caprice of hers, or whether she was trying to test me and find out if the courtship I began with your permission was meant seriously. I also thought that, if she were what she ought to be — and what we both believed her to be — she would have informed you by now of my advances. Seeing she delays, I believe the truth of the promise she has given me: that the next time you are away from the house she will grant me a meeting in the closet where your jewels are kept" — and it was true that Camilla used to meet him there — "but I don't want you to rush to take revenge, since the sin so far exists only in intention; Camilla's may change perhaps between now and the appointed time, and repentance spring up instead. So far you have always followed my advice in whole or in part — follow and observe what I will tell you now, so that, with no mistake and with mature deliberation, you can satisfy yourself as to the best course. Pretend to leave for two or three days, as you have done before, and arrange to hide yourself in the closet; the tapestries and other things there make it easy to conceal yourself. Then you will see with your own eyes, and I with mine, what Camilla's purpose is. And if it turns out guilty — which is to be feared rather than expected — then with silence, prudence, and discretion you yourself can become the instrument of punishment for the wrong done to you."

Anselmo was stunned, overwhelmed, and astounded by Lothario's words, which fell on him at a moment when he least expected to hear them, since he now thought of Camilla as having triumphed over Lothario's pretended attacks and was beginning to enjoy the glory of her victory. He sat in silence for a long time, eyes fixed on the ground, and at last said, "Lothario, you have behaved exactly as I expected your friendship to behave. I'll follow your advice in everything; do as you see fit, and keep this secret as you can see it must be kept in such unforeseen circumstances."

Lothario gave him his word, but after leaving him he regretted everything he had said, realising how foolishly he had acted — he might have revenged himself on Camilla in some less cruel and less degrading way. He cursed his lack of sense, condemned his hasty decision, and had no idea how to undo the damage or find some quick escape from it. At last he decided to tell Camilla everything, and since opportunity was not wanting, he found her alone that same day. But the moment she got a chance to speak to him she said, "Lothario my friend, I have to tell you that there's a sorrow in my heart so heavy it seems ready to burst; and it'll be a wonder if it doesn't, because Leonela's audacity has reached such a pitch that every night she hides a gallant of hers in this house and stays with him till morning, at the cost of my reputation — for anyone who sees him leaving my house at such unseasonable hours is free to question it. What distresses me is that I can't punish or scold her, since her knowledge of our affair gags me and keeps me silent about hers; and I dread that some catastrophe will come of it."

As Camilla said this, Lothario at first imagined it was some trick to make him believe that the man he had seen leaving was Leonela's lover and not hers; but when he saw how she wept and suffered, and begged him to help her, he was convinced of the truth, and the conviction completed his confusion and remorse. Even so, he told Camilla not to distress herself, since he would take steps to put a stop to Leonela's insolence. At the same time he told her what, driven by the savage rage of jealousy, he had said to Anselmo, and how he had arranged to hide in the closet to see for himself how little she preserved her loyalty to him; and he begged her forgiveness for this madness, and her advice on how to repair it and escape safely from the tangled labyrinth his imprudence had landed him in. Camilla was struck with alarm at hearing what Lothario said, and with much anger and great good sense she reproved him and rebuked his base scheme and the foolish, mischievous decision he had made. But as woman has by nature a quicker wit than man for good or evil, though it tends to fail when she sets herself deliberately to reason, Camilla on the spot thought of a way to remedy what looked irremediable, and told Lothario to arrange that the next day Anselmo should hide in the place he had mentioned, since she hoped, through that concealment, to find the means by which they could enjoy themselves in the future with no fear; and without revealing her purpose to him in full, she instructed him to be ready, as soon as Anselmo was hidden, to come to her when Leonela called him, and to answer everything she said to him as he would have answered had he not known Anselmo was listening. Lothario pressed her to explain her plan in full, so that he could with more certainty and caution do whatever was needed.

"I tell you," said Camilla, "there's nothing to take care of except to answer me what I ask you;" for she didn't want to explain to him beforehand what she meant to do, afraid he wouldn't go along with an idea that seemed to her so good, and would try to come up with some other less practical plan.

Lothario then withdrew, and the next day Anselmo, on the pretext of going to his friend's country house, set off and then returned to hide — which he was able to do easily, since Camilla and Leonela took care to give him the opportunity. So he settled himself in his hiding place in the state of agitation you can imagine in a man expecting to see the vitals of his honour laid bare before his eyes, on the brink of losing the supreme blessing he thought he possessed in his beloved Camilla. Once they had made sure Anselmo was in his hiding place, Camilla and Leonela entered the closet, and the instant she set foot inside Camilla said, with a deep sigh, "Ah! dear Leonela, wouldn't it be better, before I do what I don't want you to know lest you try to prevent it, that you take Anselmo's dagger that I asked you for and run it through this vile heart of mine? But no — there's no reason why I should suffer the punishment for someone else's fault. I'll first find out what it is that the bold, lecherous eyes of Lothario have seen in me that could have encouraged him to reveal to me a design as base as the one he has disclosed, with no regard for his friend or for my honour. Go to the window, Leonela, and call him, for no doubt he's down in the street waiting to carry out his vile project; but mine — cruel as it may be, but honourable — shall be carried out first."

"Oh, señora," said the crafty Leonela, who knew her part, "what is it you mean to do with this dagger? Can it be that you mean to take your own life, or Lothario's? Whichever you mean, it will lead to the loss of your reputation and good name. It would be better to swallow the wrong and not give this wicked man the chance to come into the house now and find us alone; remember, señora, we are weak women, and he is a man, and a determined one, and as he's coming with such a base purpose, blind and driven by passion, perhaps before you can carry out yours he'll do what will be worse for you than taking your life. A curse on my master, Anselmo, for giving such authority in his house to this shameless creature! And suppose you do kill him, señora, as I suspect you mean to — what do we do with him when he's dead?"

"What, my friend?" replied Camilla. "We'll leave him for Anselmo to bury, for it stands to reason it'll be a light task for him to hide his own infamy underground. Summon him, hurry, for every moment I delay in taking revenge for my wrong feels like an offence against the loyalty I owe my husband."

Anselmo was listening to all this, and every word Camilla uttered changed his mind further; but when he heard that she was resolved to kill Lothario his first impulse was to come out and show himself to head off such a disaster. Yet in his eagerness to see how a resolution so bold and virtuous would play out, he held himself back, intending to come forward in time to prevent the deed. At this moment Camilla threw herself onto a bed that stood nearby and swooned away, and Leonela began to weep bitterly, exclaiming, "Oh, woe is me, that I should be fated to have dying here in my arms the flower of virtue on earth, the crown of true wives, the very pattern of chastity!" — and more in the same vein, so that anyone hearing her would have taken her for the most tender-hearted and faithful handmaid in the world, and her mistress for another persecuted Penelope.

Camilla was not long in recovering from her faint, and on coming to herself she said, "Why don't you go, Leonela, and call here that friend, the falsest the sun ever shone upon or night ever concealed? Away, run, hurry, fly! lest the fire of my wrath burn itself out with delay, and the righteous vengeance I am hoping for melt away into mere threats and curses."

"I'm going right now to call him, señora," said Leonela; "but first you must give me that dagger, lest while I'm gone you use it to give cause to all who love you to weep for the rest of their lives."

"Go in peace, dear Leonela, I won't," said Camilla; "for rash and foolish as I may seem to you in defending my honour, I'm not going to be as much so as that Lucretia who they say killed herself without having done anything wrong, and without first killing the man on whom the guilt of her misfortune lay. I shall die, if I am to die — but it has to be after taking full revenge on the man who has brought me to this point, to weep over an audacity that no fault of mine gave rise to."

Leonela needed much pressing before she would go to summon Lothario, but at last she went, and while waiting for her to return Camilla continued, as if speaking to herself, "Good God! wouldn't it have been more sensible to keep on repulsing Lothario, as I've done many a time, than to allow him, as I'm now doing, to think me unchaste and vile, even for the short time I have to wait before undeceiving him? No doubt it would have been better; but then I should not be avenged, nor my husband's honour vindicated, if he should find so clean and easy an escape from the strait into which his depravity has led him. Let the traitor pay with his life for the temerity of his wanton wishes, and let the world know — if ever it does come to know — that Camilla not only preserved her loyalty to her husband but avenged him on the man who dared to wrong him. Still, I think it might be better to disclose this to Anselmo. But I did already call his attention to it in the letter I wrote him in the country, and if he did nothing to prevent the harm I pointed out there, I suppose it was that out of pure goodness of heart and trust he would not and could not believe that any thought against his honour could lodge in the breast of so steadfast a friend; nor did I myself believe it for many days, nor should I ever have believed it if his insolence had not gone so far as to make it plain through open presents, lavish promises, and ceaseless tears. But why am I arguing this way? Does a bold decision need arguments? Surely not. Then away with traitors! Vengeance, to my aid! Let the false one come, approach, advance, die, give up his life, and then come what may. Pure I came to the man Heaven gave me; pure I shall leave him — and at the worst, bathed in my own chaste blood and in the foul blood of the falsest friend that friendship ever saw in the world." And as she uttered these words she paced the room holding the unsheathed dagger, with such irregular, disordered steps and such gestures that one would have thought she had lost her senses and taken her for some violent desperado rather than a delicate woman.

Anselmo, concealed behind some tapestries where he had hidden himself, watched and was amazed at it all; and he already felt that what he had seen and heard was a sufficient answer to even greater suspicions. He would have been quite content now to skip the further proof of Lothario's coming, since he feared some sudden mishap; but just as he was about to show himself and come out to embrace his wife and undeceive her, he paused, seeing Leonela returning, leading Lothario. Camilla, when she saw him, drew a long line on the floor in front of her with the dagger and said to him, "Lothario, pay attention to what I say to you: if by any chance you dare to cross this line you see, or even approach it, the instant I see you try it I will run this dagger I'm holding through my own breast. And before you answer me a word I want you to listen to a few from me, after which you may reply as you please. First, I want you to tell me, Lothario, whether you know my husband Anselmo, and in what light you regard him; and second, I want to know whether you also know me. Answer me without embarrassment or pondering at length what to say, for these are no riddles I'm putting to you."

Lothario was not so slow that, from the first moment Camilla told him to have Anselmo hide himself, he hadn't understood what she meant to do; and so he fell in with her idea so promptly and readily that between them they made the deception look truer than truth. He answered her like this: "I did not think, fair Camilla, that you were calling me to ask questions so far removed from the purpose for which I came; but if it's to delay the promised reward you're doing so, you might have put it off still longer, for the longing for happiness brings the greater distress the nearer the hope of attaining it comes. But lest you say I don't answer your questions, I say that I do know your husband Anselmo, and that we have known each other from our earliest years; I won't speak of what you also know — of our friendship — that I may not compel myself to testify against the wrong that love, the great excuse for greater errors, is making me do to him. You I know, and I hold in the same esteem as he does, for were it not so I would not for a lesser prize have acted against what I owe to my station and the holy laws of true friendship, now broken and violated by me through that powerful enemy, love."

"If you confess that," Camilla returned, "mortal enemy of all that rightly deserves to be loved, with what face do you dare to come before the woman you know to be the mirror in which he is reflected, in whom you should look to see how unworthily you wrong him? But, woe is me, I now understand what made you give so little heed to what you owe to yourself; it must have been some freedom of mine — I will not call it immodesty, since it did not come from any deliberate intention but from some carelessness that women are guilty of through inadvertence when they think they have no need to be on guard. But tell me, traitor, when did I, by word or sign, give a reply to your prayers that could awaken in you the shadow of a hope of attaining your base wishes? When were your professions of love not sternly and scornfully rejected and rebuked? When were your frequent pledges, and your still more frequent gifts, believed or accepted? But since I am persuaded that no one can long persevere in trying to win love unsustained by some hope, I am willing to take upon myself the blame for your presumption, for no doubt some thoughtlessness of mine has all this time fed your hopes; and therefore I will punish myself and inflict on myself the penalty your guilt deserves. And so that you may see that being so merciless to myself I cannot possibly be otherwise to you, I have summoned you to be a witness of the sacrifice I mean to offer to the injured honour of my honoured husband, wronged by you with all the persistence you were capable of, and by me too through lack of caution in avoiding every occasion — if I ever gave any — of encouraging and sanctioning your base designs. Once more I say: the suspicion in my mind that some imprudence of mine has engendered these lawless thoughts in you is what distresses me most, and what I most desire to punish with my own hands; for were any other instrument of punishment used, my error might become perhaps more widely known. But before I do so, in my death I mean to inflict death, and take with me one that will fully satisfy my longing for the revenge I hope for and shall have; for I shall see, wherever I go, the penalty awarded by inflexible, unswerving justice on the man who has placed me in so desperate a position."

As she said these words, with incredible energy and speed she flew at Lothario with the naked dagger, so obviously bent on burying it in his breast that he was almost uncertain whether her display was real or feigned; and he had to use all his skill and strength to keep her from striking him. So convincingly did she play this strange charade and mystification that, to give it a touch of truth, she decided to stain it with her own blood; for finding — or pretending — that she could not wound Lothario, she said, "It seems Fate will not grant my just desire complete satisfaction, but it will not be able to keep me from satisfying it at least in part;" and making an effort to free the hand with the dagger that Lothario was holding, she pulled it loose, and aiming the point at a place where it could not inflict a deep wound, she plunged it into her left side high up near the shoulder, then let herself fall to the floor as if in a faint.

Leonela and Lothario stood amazed and astounded at the turn of events, and seeing Camilla stretched on the ground and bathed in her blood they were still uncertain as to the true nature of what had happened. Lothario, terrified and breathless, rushed to pluck the dagger out; but when he saw how slight the wound was he was relieved of his fears, and once more he admired the subtlety, coolness, and ready wit of the fair Camilla. And the better to support the part he had to play, he began to pour out profuse, doleful lamentations over her body as if she were dead, invoking curses not only on himself but also on the man who had been the cause of placing him in such a position: knowing that his friend Anselmo could hear him, he spoke in such a way as to make any listener feel much more pity for him than for Camilla, even though they took her for dead. Leonela picked her up in her arms and laid her on the bed, begging Lothario to go and find someone to tend to the wound in secret, and at the same time asking his advice and opinion as to what they should tell Anselmo about his lady's wound if he should happen to come back before it was healed. He answered that they might say what they liked, for he was in no state to give useful advice; all he could tell her was to try to staunch the blood, since he was going where he would never be seen again. With every appearance of deep grief and sorrow he left the house; but once he found himself alone, where there was nobody to see him, he crossed himself unceasingly, lost in wonder at Camilla's adroitness and the consistent acting of Leonela. He reflected on how convinced Anselmo would be that he had a second Portia for a wife, and looked forward eagerly to meeting him so they could rejoice together over the most cunningly veiled falsehood and truth one could imagine.

Leonela, as he had told her, staunched her lady's blood — which was no more than was needed to support the deception — and washing the wound with a little wine she bandaged it as best she could, talking all the while she was tending her in a vein that, even if nothing else had been said before, would have been enough to assure Anselmo that he had in Camilla a model of purity. To Leonela's words Camilla added her own, calling herself a coward and lacking in spirit, since she had not had enough of it at the moment she most needed it to rid herself of the life she so much loathed. She asked her attendant's advice as to whether or not she ought to tell her beloved husband everything that had happened, but Leonela told her to say nothing about it, since she would be laying on him the obligation of taking vengeance on Lothario — which he could not do without great risk to himself — and it was the duty of a true wife not to give her husband cause to quarrel, but, on the contrary, to remove every such cause as far from him as possible.

Camilla replied that she thought Leonela was right and that she would follow her advice, but in any case it would be wise to think how she was to explain the wound to Anselmo, since he could not help seeing it; to which Leonela answered that she didn't know how to tell a lie even in jest.

"Then how can I know how, my dear?" said Camilla; "for I wouldn't dare to invent or keep up a falsehood if my life depended on it. If we can think of no way out of this difficulty, it would be better to tell him the plain truth than to be caught out in a made-up story."

"Don't worry, señora," said Leonela; "between now and tomorrow I'll think of what we should tell him, and perhaps with the wound being where it is it can be hidden from his sight, and Heaven will be pleased to aid us in a purpose so good and honourable. Calm yourself, señora, and try to settle your nerves so my lord doesn't find you agitated; leave the rest to my care and God's, who always supports good intentions."

Anselmo had listened with the deepest attention to, and seen played out, the tragedy of the death of his honour, performed by the actors with such wonderfully effective truth that it seemed they had become the very characters they were playing. He longed for night and a chance to escape the house to go see his good friend Lothario, and with him pour out his joy over the precious pearl he had gained in having confirmed his wife's purity. Both mistress and maid took care to give him time and opportunity to slip away, and seizing it he made his escape and went straight in search of Lothario. It would be impossible to describe how he embraced him when he found him, and the things he said in his heart's joy, and the praises he heaped on Camilla; all of which Lothario listened to without being able to show any pleasure, since he could not forget how deceived his friend was and how dishonourably he had wronged him. And though Anselmo could see that Lothario was not happy, he imagined it was only because he had left Camilla wounded and had been the cause of it; and so among other things he told him not to be distressed about Camilla's accident — since, as they had agreed to hide it from him, the wound was clearly trifling, and so he had no cause for fear, but should from now on be of good cheer and rejoice with him, seeing that by his means and adroitness he found himself raised to the greatest height of happiness he could have hoped for. He wanted no better pastime than writing verses in praise of Camilla that would preserve her name for all time. Lothario commended the plan, and promised on his own part to help him raise a monument so glorious.

And so Anselmo was left the most charmingly hoodwinked man there could be in the world. He himself, convinced he was leading the instrument of his glory, was led home by the hand of the man who had been the utter ruin of his good name; whom Camilla received with averted face but smiles in her heart. The deception was kept up for some time, until at the end of a few months Fortune turned her wheel and the guilt that had until then been so skilfully hidden was published abroad, and Anselmo paid with his life the penalty of his ill-advised curiosity.

title: Part 1, Chapter 35
paragraphs: About the heroic and prodigious battle Don Quixote had with certain skins of red wine, and which brings the novel of "The Ill-Advised Curiosity" to a close

Little of the novel remained to be read when Sancho Panza came bursting in wild excitement out of the garret where Don Quixote was lying, shouting, "Run, sirs! quick — help my master, who's in the thick of the toughest and stiffest battle I ever laid eyes on. By the living God, he has given the giant — the enemy of my lady the Princess Micomicona — such a slash that he has sliced his head clean off as if it were a turnip."

"What are you talking about, brother?" said the curate, pausing as he was about to read the rest of the novel. "Are you in your senses, Sancho? How the devil can it be as you say, when the giant is two thousand leagues away?"

Just then they heard a loud noise in the chamber, and Don Quixote shouting, "Stand, thief, brigand, villain! I have you now, and your scimitar won't help you!" And it sounded as if he were slashing vigorously at the wall.

"Don't stop to listen," said Sancho, "but go in and break them up, or help my master — though there's no need of that now, for no doubt the giant is dead by this time and giving account to God of his past wicked life; for I saw the blood flowing on the ground, and the head cut off and fallen on one side, and it's as big as a large wine-skin."

"May I die," said the landlord at that, "if Don Quixote or Don Devil hasn't been slashing some of the skins of red wine that stand full at the head of his bed, and the spilled wine is what this good fellow takes for blood." Saying this he went into the room and the rest after him, and there they found Don Quixote in the strangest outfit in the world. He was in his shirt, which wasn't long enough in front to cover his thighs completely and was six fingers shorter behind; his legs were very long and lean, covered with hair, and anything but clean; on his head he had a little greasy red cap that belonged to the host; around his left arm he had rolled the blanket of the bed — to which Sancho, for reasons best known to himself, bore a grudge — and in his right hand he held his drawn sword, with which he was slashing about on all sides, shouting exclamations as if he were really fighting some giant; and the best of it was, his eyes were not open — he was fast asleep, and dreaming that he was doing battle with the giant. For his imagination was so worked upon by the adventure he was going to accomplish that it made him dream he had already reached the kingdom of Micomicon and was engaged in combat with his enemy; and believing he was laying into the giant, he had given the wine-skins so many sword-cuts that the whole room was awash with wine. Seeing this, the landlord was so enraged that he fell on Don Quixote, and with his clenched fist began to pummel him in such a way that if Cardenio and the curate had not dragged him off he would have brought the war of the giant to an end. In spite of all this the poor gentleman never woke until the barber brought a great pot of cold water from the well and flung it in one dash over his body, at which Don Quixote woke up — but not so completely as to grasp what was going on. Dorothea, seeing how short and slight his outfit was, refused to go in and watch the battle between her champion and her opponent. As for Sancho, he went searching all over the floor for the head of the giant, and not finding it he said, "Now I see it's all enchantment in this house; for last time, on this very spot where I am now, I got ever so many thumps without knowing who gave them to me or being able to see anyone; and now this head is nowhere to be seen, though I saw it cut off with my own eyes and the blood running from the body as if from a fountain."

"What blood and fountains are you talking about, enemy of God and his saints?" said the landlord. "Don't you see, you thief, that the blood and the fountain are only these skins here that have been stabbed, and the red wine swimming all over the room? — and I wish I saw the soul of the man who stabbed them swimming in hell."

"I know nothing about that," said Sancho; "all I know is it will be my bad luck that, by not finding this head, my county will melt away like salt in water" — for Sancho awake was worse than his master asleep, so much had his master's promises addled his wits.

The landlord was beside himself at the squire's coolness and the master's mischief, and swore it would not be like the last time when they went off without paying; and that this time their privileges of chivalry wouldn't hold good and let one or the other of them off without paying, right down to the cost of the plugs that would have to be put in the damaged wine-skins. The curate was holding Don Quixote's hands; and Don Quixote, fancying he had now finished the adventure and was in the presence of the Princess Micomicona, knelt before the curate and said, "Exalted and beauteous lady, your highness may live from this day forth with no fear of any harm this base being could do you; and I too from this day forth am released from the promise I gave you, since by the help of God on high and by the favour of her by whom I live and breathe, I have fulfilled it so successfully."
"Didn't I say so?" said Sancho on hearing this. "You see I wasn't drunk; you see my master has already salted the giant; there's no doubt about the bulls; my county is all right!"

Who could have helped laughing at the absurdities of the pair, master and man? And laugh they did, all except the landlord, who was cursing himself. But in the end the barber, Cardenio, and the curate, with no small trouble, managed to get Don Quixote on the bed, where he fell asleep with every appearance of utter exhaustion. They left him to sleep and came out to the inn gate to console Sancho Panza for not having found the giant's head; but they had much more work appeasing the landlord, who was furious at the sudden death of his wine-skins. The landlady, half scolding, half crying, said, "In an evil moment and at an unlucky hour he came into my house, this knight-errant — I wish I'd never set eyes on him, for he's cost me dear. Last time he went off with the overnight bill against him for supper, bed, straw, and barley for himself and his squire and a hack and an ass, saying he was a knight-adventurer — God send unlucky adventures to him and to all the adventurers in the world! — and so wasn't bound to pay anything, since it was settled that way by the knight-errantry tariff. And then, all because of him, came the other gentleman and carried off my tail, and gives it back more than two cuartillos the worse, all stripped of its hair, so it's no use for my husband's purpose; and then, for the finishing touch, to burst my wine-skins and spill my wine! I wish I saw his own blood spilt! But he needn't fool himself, because by the bones of my father and the shade of my mother, they shall pay me down every quarto, or my name is not what it is, and I am not my father's daughter." All this and more in the same vein the landlady delivered with great irritation, and her good maid Maritornes backed her up, while the daughter held her peace and smiled from time to time. The curate smoothed matters by promising to make good all losses to the best of his power — not only for the wine-skins, but also the wine, and above all the depreciation of the tail they set such store by. Dorothea consoled Sancho, telling him she promised that as soon as it became certain his master had decapitated the giant, and she found herself peacefully established in her kingdom, she would bestow on him the best county in it. With this Sancho was consoled, and assured the princess she could rely on it that he had seen the head of the giant, and what's more it had a beard that reached to the girdle, and if it wasn't to be seen now it was because everything that happened in that house went by enchantment, as he himself had proved the last time he had lodged there. Dorothea said she fully believed him, and that he needn't be uneasy, since all would go well and turn out as he wished. Now that everyone was appeased, the curate was eager to go on with the novel, since he saw there was not much left to read. Dorothea and the others begged him to finish it, and he, willing to please them and enjoying reading it himself, continued the tale in these words:

The result was that, from the confidence Anselmo felt in Camilla's virtue, he lived happy and free from anxiety; and Camilla deliberately looked coldly on Lothario, so Anselmo would suppose her feelings toward him to be the opposite of what they really were. To support the position better, Lothario begged to be excused from coming to the house, since the displeasure with which Camilla regarded his presence was plain to see. But the duped Anselmo would on no account allow such a thing, and so in a thousand ways he became the author of his own dishonour while he believed he was insuring his happiness. Meanwhile the satisfaction with which Leonela saw herself empowered to carry on her own affair reached such a pitch that, regardless of everything else, she followed her inclinations without restraint, confident that her mistress would cover for her, and even show her how to manage it safely. At last one night Anselmo heard footsteps in Leonela's room, and on trying to enter to see who was there, he found the door was held against him — which made him all the more determined to open it. Forcing it open, he entered the room in time to see a man leaping out the window into the street. He ran quickly to catch him or find out who he was, but he couldn't do either, because Leonela flung her arms around him crying, "Be calm, señor; don't give way to passion or chase after the man who has escaped from here. He belongs to me — in fact, he is my husband."

Anselmo wouldn't believe it; blind with rage, he drew a dagger and threatened to stab Leonela, ordering her to tell the truth or he would kill her. In her terror, not knowing what she was saying, she exclaimed, "Don't kill me, señor, for I can tell you things more important than anything you can imagine."
"Tell me then, at once, or you die," said Anselmo.

"It would be impossible for me now," said Leonela; "I'm so agitated. Leave me till tomorrow, and then you shall hear from me what will astonish you; but rest assured the man who leaped out the window is a young man of this city who has given me his promise to marry me."

Anselmo was appeased with this and was content to wait the time she asked, for he never expected to hear anything against Camilla, so satisfied and sure of her virtue was he. So he left the room, locking Leonela in, telling her she would not come out until she had told him everything she had to make known. He went at once to see Camilla, and told her, as he did, everything that had passed between him and her handmaid, and the promise she had given to inform him of matters of serious importance.

There's no need to say whether Camilla was agitated or not, for so great were her fear and dismay that, making certain — as she had good reason to do — that Leonela would tell Anselmo all she knew of her unfaithfulness, she didn't have the courage to wait and see if her suspicions were confirmed. That same night, as soon as she thought Anselmo was asleep, she packed up the most valuable jewels she had and some money, and without being seen by anyone slipped out of the house and made her way to Lothario's. There she told him what had happened and begged him either to convey her to some place of safety or to fly with her where they would be safe from Anselmo. The perplexity into which Camilla threw Lothario was such that he could not utter a word in reply, much less decide what he should do. In the end he resolved to take her to a convent where one of his sisters was prioress. Camilla agreed, and with the speed the circumstances demanded, Lothario took her to the convent, left her there, and then himself left the city without letting anyone know of his departure.

As soon as daylight came, Anselmo, without missing Camilla from his side, rose eager to learn what Leonela had to tell him, and hurried to the room where he had locked her in. He opened the door, entered, but found no Leonela; all he found was some sheets knotted to the window — plain proof that she had let herself down from it and escaped. He returned, uneasy, to tell Camilla, but not finding her in bed or anywhere in the house he was lost in amazement. He questioned the servants, but none of them could explain. As he was going in search of Camilla, he chanced to notice her boxes lying open, and that most of her jewels were gone; and now he became fully aware of his disgrace, and that Leonela was not the cause of his misfortune. Just as he was, without stopping to dress completely, sad at heart and dejected, he went to his friend Lothario to pour out his sorrow to him; but when he failed to find him, and the servants reported that he had been absent from his house all night and had taken all his money with him, Anselmo felt as if he were losing his mind. And to top it all off, on returning to his own house he found it deserted and empty, with not a single servant, male or female, remaining. He didn't know what to think, or say, or do, and his reason seemed to be slipping away little by little. He took stock of his position, and saw himself in a moment left without wife, friend, or servants — abandoned, as he felt, by the heaven above him, and more than anything robbed of his honour, for in Camilla's disappearance he saw his own ruin. After long reflection he at last resolved to go to his friend's village, where he had been staying when he provided the opportunity for the contrivance of this whole tangle of misfortune. He locked the doors of his house, mounted his horse, and with a broken spirit set out on his journey. But he had hardly gone halfway when, harassed by his thoughts, he had to dismount and tie his horse to a tree, at the foot of which he threw himself down, giving vent to pitiful, heartrending sighs; and there he remained till nearly nightfall, when he saw a man approaching on horseback from the city, of whom, after greeting him, he asked what news there was in Florence.

The citizen replied, "The strangest that has been heard for many a day; for it's being reported abroad that Lothario, the great friend of the wealthy Anselmo, who lived at San Giovanni, last night carried off Camilla, the wife of Anselmo, who has also disappeared. All this was told by a maid of Camilla's, whom the governor caught last night lowering herself by a sheet from the windows of Anselmo's house. I don't know exactly how the affair came about; all I know is that the whole city is wondering at it, for no one could have expected anything of the kind, given the great and intimate friendship between them, so great they say they were called 'The Two Friends.'"
"Is it known at all," said Anselmo, "what road Lothario and Camilla took?"
"Not in the least," said the citizen, "though the governor has been very active in searching for them."
"God speed you, señor," said Anselmo.
"God be with you," said the citizen, and went his way.

This disastrous news almost robbed Anselmo not only of his wits but of his life. He got up as well as he could and reached the house of his friend, who as yet knew nothing of his misfortune, but seeing him come in pale, worn, and haggard, perceived he was suffering some heavy affliction. Anselmo at once begged to be allowed to retire to rest, and to be given writing materials. His wish was granted and he was left lying down and alone, since he asked for that, and even that the door be locked. Finding himself alone, he so took to heart the thought of his misfortune that, by the signs of death he felt within him, he knew well his life was drawing to a close, and therefore he resolved to leave behind a declaration of the cause of his strange end. He began to write, but before he could put down all he meant to say his breath failed him and he yielded up his life, a victim of the suffering his ill-advised curiosity had brought upon him. The master of the house, seeing that it was now late and Anselmo had not called, decided to go in and find out if his indisposition was getting worse, and found him lying on his face, his body partly on the bed and partly on the writing-table, on which he lay with the written paper open and the pen still in his hand. Having first called him without receiving any answer, his host went over to him, and taking him by the hand, found it cold and saw he was dead. Greatly surprised and distressed, he summoned the household to witness the sad fate that had befallen Anselmo; and then he read the paper, the handwriting of which he recognised as Anselmo's, and which contained these words:

"A foolish and ill-advised desire has robbed me of life. If the news of my death should reach Camilla's ears, let her know that I forgive her, for she was not bound to perform miracles, nor ought I to have required her to perform them; and since I have been the author of my own dishonour, there is no reason why —"

So far Anselmo had written, and so it was plain that at this point, before he could finish what he had to say, his life came to an end. The next day his friend sent word of his death to his relatives, who had already learned of his misfortune, as well as to the convent where Camilla lay almost on the point of accompanying her husband on that inevitable journey — not on account of the tidings of his death, but because of those she had received of her lover's departure. Although she found herself a widow, it is said she refused either to leave the convent or to take the veil, until, not long afterwards, news reached her that Lothario had been killed in a battle in which M. de Lautrec had recently been engaged with the Great Captain Gonzalo Fernandez de Cordova in the kingdom of Naples, where her too-late repentant lover had gone. On hearing this Camilla took the veil, and shortly afterwards died, worn out by grief and melancholy. This was the end of all three, an end that came of a thoughtless beginning.

"I like this novel," said the curate; "but I can't persuade myself of its truth; and if it has been invented, the author's invention is faulty, for it's impossible to imagine any husband foolish enough to try such a costly experiment as Anselmo's. If it had been told as occurring between a gallant and his mistress, it might pass; but between husband and wife there's something of an impossibility about it. As to the way the story is told, however, I have no fault to find."

title: Part 1, Chapter 36
paragraphs: About more curious incidents that occurred at the inn
Just at that instant the landlord, who was standing at the gate of the inn, exclaimed, "Here comes a fine troop of guests; if they stop here we may say _gaudeamus_."
"Who are they?" said Cardenio.

"Four men," said the landlord, "riding _à la jineta_, with lances and bucklers, all with black veils; and with them there's a woman in white on a side-saddle, whose face is also veiled, and two attendants on foot."
"Are they very near?" said the curate.
"So near," answered the landlord, "that here they come."

Hearing this, Dorothea covered her face and Cardenio retreated into Don Quixote's room, and they hardly had time to do so before the whole party the host had described entered the inn. The four on horseback, of well-bred appearance and bearing, dismounted and came forward to take down the woman who was riding on the side-saddle; and one of them, taking her in his arms, placed her in a chair that stood at the entrance of the room where Cardenio had hidden himself. All this time neither she nor they had removed their veils or spoken a word; only on sitting down on the chair did the woman give a deep sigh and let her arms fall like one who was ill and weak. The attendants on foot then led the horses away to the stable. Watching this, the curate, curious to know who these people in such dress and preserving such silence might be, went to where the servants were standing and put the question to one of them, who answered him.

"Faith, sir, I can't tell you who they are; I only know they seem to be people of distinction, especially the one who stepped forward to take the lady you saw in his arms; and I say so because all the rest show him respect, and nothing is done except what he directs and orders."
"And the lady, who is she?" the curate asked.

"That I can't tell you either," said the servant, "for I haven't seen her face the whole way. I've heard her sigh many times and utter such groans she seems to be giving up the ghost every time; but it's no wonder we don't know more than we've told you, since my comrade and I have only been in their company two days — they met us on the road and begged and persuaded us to accompany them to Andalusia, promising to pay us well."
"And have you heard any of them called by name?" asked the curate.

"No, indeed," the servant replied; "they all keep up a marvellous silence on the road, for not a sound is to be heard among them except the poor lady's sighs and sobs, which make us pity her. We feel sure that wherever it is she's going, she's going against her will; and as far as one can judge from her dress, she's a nun, or — what's more likely — about to become one. Perhaps it's because taking the vows isn't of her own free will that she's as unhappy as she seems."

"That may well be," said the curate, and leaving them he returned to where Dorothea was. Dorothea, hearing the veiled lady sigh, moved by natural compassion, drew near to her and said, "What are you suffering from, señora? If it's anything that women are accustomed and know how to relieve, I offer you my services with all my heart."

To this the unhappy lady made no reply; and though Dorothea repeated her offers more earnestly, she still kept silent, until the gentleman with the veil — the one the servant said was obeyed by the rest — approached and said to Dorothea, "Don't trouble yourself, señora, to make offers to that woman, for it's her way to give no thanks for anything done for her; and don't try to make her answer unless you want to hear some lie from her lips."

"I've never told a lie," was the immediate reply of the woman who had been silent until then; "on the contrary, it's because I am so truthful and so ignorant of lying ways that I'm now in this miserable condition; and this I call on you yourself to witness, since it is my unstained truth that has made you false and a liar."

Cardenio heard these words clearly and distinctly, being right next to the speaker — for only the door of Don Quixote's room stood between them — and the instant he heard them, uttering a loud exclamation he cried, "Good God! what is this I hear? What voice is this that has reached my ears?" Startled at the voice, the lady turned her head; and not seeing the speaker she stood up and tried to enter the room. Seeing this, the gentleman held her back, preventing her from moving a step. In her agitation and sudden movement, the silk with which she had covered her face fell off and disclosed a countenance of incomparable, marvellous beauty, but pale and terrified, for she kept turning her eyes — everywhere she could direct her gaze — with an eagerness that made her look as if she had lost her senses, and so markedly that it stirred the pity of Dorothea and all who saw her, though they did not know what caused it. The gentleman grasped her firmly by the shoulders, and being so fully occupied with holding her back, he was unable to put a hand to his own veil, which was slipping off — and at length did fall off completely. Dorothea, who was holding the lady in her arms, raising her eyes saw that the man who also held her was her husband, Don Fernando. The instant she recognised him, with a long, plaintive cry drawn from the depths of her heart, she fell backwards in a faint; and but for the barber being close by to catch her in his arms, she would have fallen full-length to the ground. The curate at once hurried to uncover her face and throw water on it; and as he did so, Don Fernando — for it was he who held the other in his arms — recognised her and stood as if struck dead by the sight; not, however, relaxing his grasp on Luscinda, for it was she who was struggling to release herself from his hold, having recognised Cardenio by his voice as he had recognised her. Cardenio also heard Dorothea's cry as she fell fainting, and imagining that it came from his Luscinda, burst forth in terror from the room, and the first thing he saw was Don Fernando with Luscinda in his arms. Don Fernando too recognised Cardenio at once; and all three — Luscinda, Cardenio, and Dorothea — stood in silent astonishment, scarcely knowing what had happened to them.

They gazed at one another without speaking — Dorothea at Don Fernando, Don Fernando at Cardenio, Cardenio at Luscinda, and Luscinda at Cardenio. The first to break the silence was Luscinda, who addressed Don Fernando: "Leave me, Señor Don Fernando, for the sake of what you owe to yourself; if no other reason will move you, leave me to cling to the wall whose ivy I am, to the support from which neither your importunities, your threats, your promises, nor your gifts have been able to detach me. See how Heaven, by ways strange and hidden from our sight, has brought me face to face with my true husband; and you well know, by dear-bought experience, that death alone will be able to erase him from my memory. May this plain declaration, then, lead you — since you can do nothing else — to turn your love into rage, your affection into resentment, and so take my life; for if I yield it up in the presence of my beloved husband I count it well bestowed. By my death he may be convinced that I kept my faith to him to the last moment of life."

Meanwhile Dorothea had come to herself and had heard Luscinda's words, by which she guessed who she was; but seeing that Don Fernando did not yet release her or reply, summoning up her resolution as best she could she rose and knelt at his feet, and with a flood of bright and touching tears addressed him like this:

"If, my lord, the beams of that sun you hold eclipsed in your arms didn't dazzle and rob your eyes of sight, you would have seen by now that the woman who kneels at your feet is, so long as you will have it so, the unhappy and unfortunate Dorothea. I am that lowly peasant girl whom you, in your goodness or for your pleasure, would raise high enough to call herself yours; I am she who, in the seclusion of innocence, led a contented life until at the voice of your importunity and your true, tender passion — as it seemed — she opened the gates of her modesty and surrendered to you the keys of her liberty; a gift received by you but thanklessly, as is clearly shown by my having been forced to retreat to the place where you find me, and by your appearance here in the circumstances in which I see you. Nevertheless, I would not have you suppose that I have come here driven by my shame; it's only grief and sorrow at seeing myself forgotten by you that have brought me. It was your will to make me yours, and you so followed your will that now, even though you repent, you cannot help being mine. Consider, my lord — the unsurpassable affection I bear you may compensate for the beauty and noble birth for which you would desert me. You cannot be the fair Luscinda's, because you are mine; nor can she be yours, because she is Cardenio's; and it will be easier, remember, to bend your will to love one who adores you than to lead one to love you who detests you now. You addressed yourself to my simplicity, you laid siege to my virtue, you were not ignorant of my station, you know full well how I yielded wholly to your will; there is no ground or reason for you to plead deception. And if it be so, as it is, and if you are a Christian as you are a gentleman, why do you by such subterfuges put off making me happy at last as you did at first? And if you will not have me for what I am, your true and lawful wife, at least take and accept me as your slave; for as long as I am yours I will count myself happy and fortunate. Don't, by deserting me, let my shame become the talk of the gossips in the streets; don't make the old age of my parents miserable, for the loyal services they have always rendered yours as faithful vassals do not deserve such a return. And if you think it will debase your blood to mingle it with mine, reflect that there is little or no nobility in the world that hasn't travelled the same road, and that in illustrious lineages it isn't the woman's blood that counts; and, moreover, that true nobility consists in virtue, and if you are wanting in that — refusing me what in justice you owe me — then even I have higher claims to nobility than yours. To make an end, señor, these are my last words to you: whether you will or not, I am your wife. Witness your words, which must not and ought not to be false, if you pride yourself on that for want of which you scorn me; witness the pledge you gave me; and witness Heaven, which you yourself called to witness the promise you had made me. And if all that fails, your own conscience will not fail to lift up its silent voice in the midst of all your gaiety, to vindicate the truth of what I say and mar your highest pleasure and enjoyment."

All this and more the wronged Dorothea delivered with such earnest feeling and such tears that everyone present, even those who had come with Don Fernando, were compelled to join her in them. Don Fernando listened to her without replying, until, ceasing to speak, she gave way to such sobs and sighs that it must have been a heart of bronze that was not softened by the sight of so great a sorrow. Luscinda stood regarding her with no less compassion for her sufferings than admiration for her intelligence and beauty, and would have gone to her to say some words of comfort, but was prevented by Don Fernando's grasp, which held her fast. He, overwhelmed with confusion and astonishment, after gazing at Dorothea for some moments with a fixed stare, opened his arms, and, releasing Luscinda, exclaimed:
"You have conquered, fair Dorothea — you have conquered, for it is impossible to have the heart to deny the united force of so many truths."

Luscinda in her feebleness was on the point of falling to the ground when Don Fernando released her, but Cardenio, who stood near — having retreated behind Don Fernando to escape recognition — casting fear aside and heedless of what might happen, ran forward to support her, and as he clasped her in his arms said, "If Heaven in its compassion is willing to let you rest at last, mistress of my heart, true, constant, and fair, nowhere can you rest more safely than in these arms that now receive you, and received you before when fortune permitted me to call you mine."

At these words Luscinda looked up at Cardenio, at first beginning to recognise him by his voice and then satisfying herself by her eyes that it was he; and hardly knowing what she did, heedless of all considerations of decorum, she flung her arms around his neck and, pressing her face close to his, said, "Yes, my dear lord, you are the true master of this your slave, even though adverse fate should intervene again, and fresh dangers threaten this life that hangs on yours."

A strange sight this was for Don Fernando and those that stood around, filled with surprise at an event so unlooked-for. Dorothea fancied Don Fernando had changed colour and looked as if he meant to take vengeance on Cardenio, for she saw him put his hand to his sword; and the instant the idea struck her, with wonderful quickness she clasped him round the knees, and kissing them and holding him to prevent him from moving, she said, while her tears continued to flow, "What is it you would do, my only refuge, in this unforeseen event? You have your wife at your feet, and the woman you would have for your wife is in the arms of her husband; reflect whether it will be right for you, whether it will be possible for you, to undo what Heaven has done, or whether it will be becoming in you to seek to raise her to be your mate who, in spite of every obstacle and strong in her truth and constancy, is before your eyes, bathing with the tears of love the face and bosom of her lawful husband. For God's sake I entreat you, for your own sake I implore you, do not let this open declaration rouse your anger; rather calm it enough to allow these two lovers to live in peace and quiet without any interference from you, so long as Heaven permits them; and in doing so you will prove the generosity of your lofty noble spirit, and the world shall see that with you reason has more influence than passion."

All the time Dorothea was speaking, Cardenio, though he held Luscinda in his arms, never took his eyes off Don Fernando, determined, if he saw him make any hostile move, to try to defend himself and resist as best he could all who might assail him, even at the cost of his life. But now Don Fernando's friends, as well as the curate and the barber, who had been present all along — not forgetting the worthy Sancho Panza — ran forward and gathered round Don Fernando, begging him to have regard for Dorothea's tears, and not to let her reasonable hopes be disappointed, since, as they firmly believed, what she said was nothing but the truth; and bidding him observe that it was not, as it might seem, by accident, but by a special disposition of Providence that they had all met in a place where no one could have expected a meeting. And the curate told him to remember that only death could part Luscinda from Cardenio; that even if some sword were to separate them they would think their death most happy; and that in a case that admitted of no remedy, his wisest course was, by conquering himself and laying restraint on himself, to show a generous mind, and of his own accord let these two enjoy the happiness Heaven had granted them. He told him too to turn his eyes upon the beauty of Dorothea and he would see that few if any could equal, much less excel her, while to that beauty should be added her modesty and the surpassing love she bore him. Besides all this, he reminded him that if he prided himself on being a gentleman and a Christian, he could not do otherwise than keep his plighted word; and that in doing so he would obey God and meet the approval of all sensible people, who know and recognise it to be the privilege of beauty, even in one of humble birth — provided virtue accompany it — to be able to raise itself to the level of any rank, without any slur upon him who places it on an equality with himself; and furthermore that when the potent sway of passion asserts itself, so long as there be no mixture of sin in it, he is not to be blamed who gives way to it.

To be brief, they added such other forcible arguments that Don Fernando's manly heart, being after all nourished by noble blood, was touched, and yielded to the truth which, even had he wished, he could not gainsay; and he showed his submission, and acceptance of the good advice that had been offered, by stooping down and embracing Dorothea, saying to her, "Rise, dear lady; it is not right that what I hold in my heart should be kneeling at my feet; and if until now I have shown no sign of what I now confess, it may have been by Heaven's decree, in order that, seeing the constancy with which you love me, I may learn to value you as you deserve. What I beg of you is that you do not reproach me with my transgression and grievous wrong-doing, for the same cause and force that drove me to make you mine drove me also to struggle against being yours; and to prove this, turn and look at the eyes of the now happy Luscinda, and you will see in them an excuse for all my errors: and as she has found and gained the object of her desires, and I have found in you what satisfies all my wishes, may she live in peace and contentment as many happy years with her Cardenio as on my knees I pray Heaven to allow me to live with my Dorothea;" and with these words he once more embraced her and pressed his face to hers with such tenderness that he had to take great care to keep his tears from completing the proof of his love and repentance in the sight of all. Not so Luscinda, and Cardenio, and almost all the others, for they shed so many tears — some at their own happiness, some at that of the others — that one would have supposed a heavy calamity had fallen on them all. Even Sancho Panza was weeping; though afterwards he said he only wept because he saw that Dorothea was not, as he had fancied, the queen Micomicona, from whom he had expected such great favours. Their wonder, as well as their weeping, lasted some time, and then Cardenio and Luscinda went and fell on their knees before Don Fernando, thanking him for the favour he had done them in language so grateful he did not know how to answer them; and raising them up he embraced them with every mark of affection and courtesy.

He then asked Dorothea how she had managed to reach a place so far from her own home, and in a few fitting words she told him all that she had previously related to Cardenio, which delighted Don Fernando and his companions so much that they wished the story had been longer — so charmingly did Dorothea describe her misadventures. When she had finished, Don Fernando recounted what had befallen him in the city after he had found in Luscinda's bosom the paper in which she declared that she was Cardenio's wife and never could be his. He said he meant to kill her, and would have done so had he not been prevented by her parents; and that he quitted the house full of rage and shame, resolved to avenge himself when a more convenient opportunity should offer. The next day he learned that Luscinda had disappeared from her father's house, and no one could tell where she had gone. Finally, at the end of some months, he ascertained that she was in a convent and meant to remain there all the rest of her life if she were not to share it with Cardenio; and as soon as he had learned this, taking these three gentlemen as his companions, he arrived at the place where she was — but avoided speaking to her, fearing that if it were known he was there, stricter precautions would be taken in the convent. Watching a time when the porter's lodge was open, he left two to guard the gate, and he and the other entered the convent in search of Luscinda, whom they found in the cloisters in conversation with one of the nuns, and carrying her off without giving her time to resist they reached a place where they provided themselves with what they needed for taking her away; all of which they were able to do in complete safety, since the convent was in the country at a considerable distance from the city. He added that when Luscinda found herself in his power she lost all consciousness, and after coming round did nothing but weep and sigh without speaking a word; and so in silence and tears they reached that inn, which for him was reaching heaven, where all the mischances of earth are over and at an end.

title: Part 1, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Which continues the story of the famous Princess Micomicona, along with other comical adventures

Sancho listened to all of this with deep sorrow in his heart, watching his hopes of a title fade and vanish into smoke — the fair Princess Micomicona had turned into Dorothea, the giant into Don Fernando, while his master slept peacefully, completely unaware of everything that had happened. Dorothea could not convince herself that her present happiness was not all a dream; Cardenio was in a similar state of mind, and Luscinda's thoughts ran along the same lines.
