Don Fernando gave thanks to Heaven for the favor it had shown him and for rescuing him from the tangled labyrinth in which he had come so close to destroying both his good name and his soul; in short, everyone at the inn was full of contentment and satisfaction at the happy outcome of such a complicated and seemingly hopeless business. The priest, being a sensible man, offered sound reflections on the whole affair and congratulated each of them on their good fortune; but the person in the highest spirits and best humor was the landlady, because of the promise Cardenio and the priest had given her to pay for all the losses and damage she had suffered on Don Quixote's account. Sancho, as has already been said, was the only one who was distressed, unhappy, and dejected; and so, with a long face, he went in to his master, who had just woken up, and said to him:

"Sir Rueful Countenance, your worship can go on sleeping as long as you like, without worrying yourself about killing any giant or restoring the princess to her kingdom, because all of that is over and settled now."

"I should certainly think it is," replied Don Quixote, "because I have just fought the most enormous and astonishing battle with that giant that I can remember fighting in all the days of my life. With one backstroke — swish! — I sent his head tumbling to the ground, and so much blood gushed out of him that it ran in streams across the earth like water."

"Streams of red wine, your worship had better say," Sancho replied, "because I'll have you know, if you don't already, that the dead giant is a slashed wine-skin, the blood is the twenty-four gallons of red wine it held in its belly, the chopped-off head is the bitch who bore me — and the devil can take the whole business."
"What are you talking about, you fool?" said Don Quixote. "Have you lost your mind?"

"Get up, your worship," said Sancho, "and you'll see the fine mess you've made of things and what we'll have to pay for. You'll see the queen turned into an ordinary lady named Dorothea, and other things that will amaze you — if you can make sense of them."

"Nothing of that kind will surprise me," Don Quixote answered, "because if you remember, the last time we were here I told you that everything that happens in this place is a matter of enchantment, and it would be no wonder if the same were true now."

"I could believe all that," Sancho replied, "if my tossing in the blanket had been the same sort of thing — only it wasn't; it was real and genuine. I saw the landlord, who is here today, holding one end of the blanket and bouncing me up toward the sky very neatly and briskly, with as much laughter as muscle. And when it comes down to recognizing people, I hold for my part — simple sinner that I am — that there's no enchantment in it at all, just a lot of bruising and bad luck."
"Well, well, God will provide a remedy," said Don Quixote. "Hand me my clothes and let me go out, because I want to see these transformations and other things you're talking about."

Sancho brought him his clothes, and while he was dressing, the priest gave Don Fernando and the others present an account of Don Quixote's madness and of the trick they had used to lure him away from the Pena Pobre, where he imagined himself stationed because of his lady's scorn. He also described to them nearly all the adventures Sancho had mentioned, which amazed them and made them laugh a good deal, since it struck them, as it struck everyone, as the strangest form of madness a deranged mind could produce. But now, the priest said, since the lady Dorothea's good fortune prevented her from carrying on with their plan, they would need to invent or discover some other way of getting him home.
Cardenio proposed that they carry on with the scheme they had already started, suggesting that Luscinda could take over Dorothea's part and play it well enough.

"No," said Don Fernando, "that must not happen, because I want Dorothea to follow through with this idea of hers; and if this worthy gentleman's village is not too far away, I will be glad to do anything I can to help cure him."
"It is no more than two days' journey from here," said the priest.
"Even if it were farther," said Don Fernando, "I would gladly travel the distance for the sake of doing such a good deed."

At that moment Don Quixote came out in full armor, with Mambrino's helmet — dented as it was — on his head, his shield on his arm, and leaning on his staff, or pike. The strange figure he cut left Don Fernando and the others astonished as they took in his gaunt yellow face, half a league long, his mismatched assortment of armor, and his solemn bearing. They stood in silence, waiting to see what he would say, and he, fixing his eyes on the fair Dorothea, addressed her with great gravity and composure:

"I am informed, fair lady, by this squire of mine that your greatness has been annihilated and your very being abolished, since you have been changed from the queen and great lady you used to be into an ordinary young woman. If this was done by order of the magician king your father, out of fear that I would not give you the help you need and are entitled to, let me say that he did not and does not know half his craft, and was poorly read in the histories of chivalry. If he had read and studied them as attentively and as carefully as I have, he would have found at every turn that knights of far less renown than mine have accomplished far more difficult things. Killing some overgrown whelp of a giant is no great feat, however arrogant he may be; in fact, only a few hours ago I was locked in combat with one myself, and — I will say nothing about it, so that no one can accuse me of lying. Time, however, which reveals everything, will tell the story when we least expect it."

"You were locked in combat with a couple of wine-skins, not a giant," the landlord put in at this point; but Don Fernando told him to be quiet and on no account to interrupt Don Quixote, who went on: "I say in conclusion, high-born and disinherited lady, that if your father has brought about this transformation in your person for the reason I have given, you should attach no importance to it whatsoever; for there is no danger on earth through which my sword will not cut a path, and with that sword, before many days have passed, I will bring your enemy's head down to the ground and place the crown of your kingdom on your own."

Don Quixote said nothing more and waited for the princess's reply. She, knowing Don Fernando's determination to keep up the deception until Don Quixote had been brought home, answered with great poise and gravity: "Whoever told you, valiant Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that I had undergone any change or transformation was not telling you the truth, for I am the same person I was yesterday. It is true that certain strokes of good fortune, which have given me more than I could ever have hoped for, have made some alteration in me; but I have not on that account stopped being what I was before, or given up the desire I have held all along of relying on the strength of your valiant and invincible arm. So, señor, in your goodness, restore the father who begot me to your good opinion, and rest assured that he was a wise and prudent man, since through his art he found such a sure and easy way of remedying my misfortune; for I believe, señor, that if it had not been for you, I would never have stumbled into the good fortune I now enjoy — and in saying this I am speaking the plain truth, as most of these gentlemen here present can fully testify. All that remains is for us to set out on our journey tomorrow, since today we could not get very far; and as for the rest of the happy outcome I am counting on, I put my trust in God and in the courage of your heart."

So spoke the quick-witted Dorothea, and when he had heard her, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said to him, with a look of fury, "Now I tell you, little Sancho, you are the greatest little villain in Spain. Tell me, you thief, you vagabond — didn't you just inform me that this princess had been turned into a young woman called Dorothea, and that the head I am convinced I cut off a giant was the bitch who bore you, along with other nonsense that threw me into the worst confusion I have ever known in all my life? I swear" — and here he looked up at heaven and ground his teeth — "I have half a mind to do such damage to you as will teach sense, from now on, to every lying squire of a knight-errant in the world."

"Calm yourself, your worship, señor," Sancho answered, "for it may well be that I was mistaken about the transformation of the lady princess Micomicona. But as for the giant's head — or at any rate the stabbing of the wine-skins, and the blood being red wine — I am making no mistake there, as sure as God exists; because the wounded skins are lying right there at the head of your worship's bed, and the red wine has turned the room into a lake. If you don't believe it, you'll see when the eggs come to be fried — I mean, when his worship the landlord demands payment for all the damages. As for the rest, I am glad with all my heart that her ladyship the queen is just as she was, because it concerns me as much as it does anyone."
"I tell you again, Sancho, you are a fool," said Don Quixote. "Forgive me, and let that be the end of it."

"That is the end of it," said Don Fernando; "let us say no more about it. And since her ladyship the princess proposes to set out tomorrow, because today it is too late, so be it; we will spend the night in pleasant conversation, and tomorrow we will all accompany Señor Don Quixote, because we want to witness the valiant and unmatched deeds he is going to perform in the course of this mighty enterprise he has undertaken."

"It is I who shall serve and accompany you," said Don Quixote; "and I am deeply grateful for the favor you are granting me and the good opinion you hold of me, which I will strive to live up to, or it will cost me my life — or even more, if it could possibly cost me more."

Don Quixote and Don Fernando exchanged many compliments and courtesies, but they were cut short by a traveler who entered the inn at that moment, and whose clothing suggested a Christian recently arrived from Moorish territory: he wore a short-skirted coat of blue cloth with half-sleeves and no collar, breeches also of blue cloth, a cap of the same color, yellow buskins, and a Moorish cutlass hanging from a strap slung across his chest. Behind him, riding a donkey, came a woman dressed in Moorish style, her face veiled, a scarf on her head, wearing a small brocaded cap and a mantle that covered her from her shoulders to her feet. The man had a sturdy, well-proportioned build; he was a little over forty, somewhat dark in complexion, with a long mustache and a full beard — in short, his appearance was such that, had he been well dressed, anyone would have taken him for a person of quality and good birth. On entering he asked for a room, and when they told him there was none in the inn, he seemed distressed; going over to the woman whose dress marked her as a Moor, he lifted her down from the saddle in his arms. Luscinda, Dorothea, the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes, drawn by the strange outfit — entirely new to them — gathered around her; and Dorothea, who was always kind, courteous, and quick-witted, seeing that both the woman and the man escorting her were upset at not finding a room, said to her, "Don't be troubled, señora, by the discomfort and lack of luxuries here, for that is the way of roadside inns. Still, if you would care to share our lodging with us" — pointing to Luscinda — "you have perhaps found worse accommodation in the course of your journey."

The veiled lady made no reply to this; all she did was rise from her seat, cross her hands over her chest, bow her head, and bend her body as a sign that she was giving thanks. From her silence they concluded that she must certainly be a Moor, unable to speak a Christian language.

At this point the captive came up, having been occupied with other matters until then, and seeing them all standing around his companion while she made no reply to anything they said to her, he explained, "Ladies, this young woman barely understands my language and can speak nothing but the tongue of her own country, which is why she does not and cannot answer what has been asked of her."

"Nothing has been asked of her," Luscinda answered. "She has only been offered our company for the evening and a share of the quarters we are using, where she will be made as comfortable as the circumstances allow — with the goodwill we owe to all strangers in need of it, especially when the one being helped is a woman."

"On her behalf and my own, señora," the captive replied, "I kiss your hands, and I value highly, as I should, the favor you have offered — one which, on such an occasion and coming from persons of your evident standing, is plainly a very great one."
"Tell me, señor," said Dorothea, "is this lady a Christian or a Moor? Her dress and her silence lead us to suspect that she is what we wish she were not."
"In dress and on the outside," he said, "she is a Moor, but at heart she is a thoroughly good Christian, for she has the deepest desire to become one."
"Then she has not been baptized?" Luscinda asked.

"There has been no opportunity for that," the captive replied, "since she left Algiers, her native country and home; and so far she has not found herself in any danger of death so immediate as to make it necessary to baptize her before she has been instructed in all the ceremonies our holy mother Church requires. But, God willing, she will before long be baptized with the solemnity she deserves — a solemnity greater than her dress, or mine, would suggest."

These words made everyone who heard him eager to know who the Moorish lady and the captive were, but no one cared to ask just then, since it was clearly a better moment to help them rest than to question them about their lives. Dorothea took the Moorish lady by the hand, led her to a seat beside her own, and asked her to remove her veil. She looked at the captive as if asking him what they meant and what she should do. He told her in Arabic that they were asking her to take off her veil, and at that she removed it and revealed a face so lovely that to Dorothea she seemed more beautiful than Luscinda, and to Luscinda more beautiful than Dorothea, and all the onlookers felt that if any beauty could rival those two women's, it was the Moorish lady's — and some were even inclined to give her the edge. And since it is the privilege and charm of beauty to win hearts and attract goodwill, everyone immediately became eager to show kindness and attention to the lovely Moor.

Don Fernando asked the captive what her name was, and he answered that it was Lela Zoraida; but the moment she heard him, she guessed what the Christian had asked and said quickly, with some displeasure and force, "No, not Zoraida — Maria, Maria!" letting them understand that her name was "Maria" and not "Zoraida." These words, and the touching earnestness with which she spoke them, drew more than one tear from some of the listeners — particularly the women, who are tender-hearted and compassionate by nature. Luscinda embraced her affectionately and said, "Yes, yes — Maria, Maria," to which the Moorish lady replied, "Yes, yes, Maria; Zoraida macange," which means "not Zoraida."

Night was now coming on, and on the orders of Don Fernando's companions the landlord had taken care and trouble to prepare for them the best supper he could manage. When the hour arrived, they all sat down at a long table like one in a refectory — there was no round or square table in the inn — and the seat of honor at its head, though he tried to refuse it, they gave to Don Quixote, who asked the lady Micomicona to sit at his side, since he was her protector. Luscinda and Zoraida took the places next to her; opposite them sat Don Fernando and Cardenio, then the captive and the other gentlemen; and beside the ladies sat the priest and the barber. And so they ate their supper in high spirits, which rose even higher when they saw Don Quixote stop eating and — moved by an impulse like the one that had prompted his long speech when he dined with the goatherds — begin to address them:

"Truly, gentlemen, when you stop to think about it, the things witnessed by those who profess the order of knight-errantry are great and marvelous. Tell me: what person in this world, walking through the gate of this castle right now and seeing us as we sit here, would suppose or imagine that we are what we actually are? Who would say that this lady beside me is the great queen we all know her to be, or that I am that Knight of the Rueful Countenance whose name is trumpeted far and wide by the mouth of Fame? There can be no doubt, then, that this art and calling surpasses every other that human beings have invented, and deserves all the more honor the more it is exposed to danger. Away with anyone who claims that letters take precedence over arms; I will tell such people, whoever they may be, that they do not know what they are talking about. The reason such people usually give, and chiefly rely on, is that the labors of the mind are greater than those of the body, and that arms employ the body alone — as though the calling were a porter's trade, requiring nothing more than sturdy strength; or as though what we who profess them call arms did not include feats of vigor that demand high intelligence to carry out; or as though the mind of the warrior who has an army, or the defense of a city, in his charge did not exert itself as much as his body does. Consider whether bodily strength alone can discover or guess the enemy's intentions, his plans, his stratagems, his obstacles, or ward off looming dangers — all these are operations of the mind, in which the body plays no part whatsoever. Since arms, then, require mind just as much as letters do, let us now see which of the two minds — the scholar's or the warrior's — has the most work to do; and this will be settled by the end and goal each one aims at, for the purpose that aims at the nobler object is the more to be esteemed. The end and goal of letters — I am not speaking now of divine letters, whose aim is to lift and guide the soul to Heaven, for with an end so infinite no other can be compared — I am speaking of human letters, whose end is to establish distributive justice, to give every man what is his, and to see and make sure that good laws are observed: an end that is certainly noble, lofty, and worthy of great praise, but not of such praise as is owed to the end pursued by arms, whose object and purpose is peace, the greatest good that human beings can desire in this life. The first good news the world and mankind ever received was the news the angels brought on the night that was our day, when they sang in the air, 'Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good-will'; and the greeting that the great Master of heaven and earth taught his disciples and chosen followers to use when entering any house was to say, 'Peace be on this house'; and many other times he said to them, 'My peace I give unto you, my peace I leave you, peace be with you' — a jewel and a precious gift, given and left by such a hand, a jewel without which there can be no happiness either on earth or in heaven. This peace is the true end of war — and war is simply another name for arms. Granting, then, that the end of war is peace, and that in this it has the advantage over the end of letters, let us turn now to the bodily hardships of the man of letters and those of the man who follows the profession of arms, and see which are the greater."

Don Quixote delivered his speech in such a manner, and in such well-chosen language, that for the moment none of his listeners could possibly take him for a madman; on the contrary, since most of them were gentlemen, to whom arms belong by birthright, they listened to him with great pleasure as he continued: "Here, then, I say, is what the student has to endure. First of all, poverty — not that all students are poor, but to put the case in its most extreme form — and once I have said that he endures poverty, I think nothing more needs to be said about his hard lot, for whoever is poor has no share in the good things of life. He suffers this poverty in various forms: hunger, or cold, or lack of clothing, or all of them at once. Even so, it is never so extreme that he gets nothing at all to eat, though the meal may come at odd hours and from the leftovers of the rich; for the deepest misery of students is what they themselves call 'going out for soup,' and there is always some neighbor's brazier or hearth for them which, if it does not warm them, at least takes the edge off the cold; and finally, at night they sleep in comfort under a roof. I will not go into other details — the shortage of shirts, for instance, and the absence of any surplus of shoes, the thin and threadbare clothing, and the way they gorge themselves to bursting when good luck happens to set a banquet of some kind before them. By this road I have described — rough and hard, stumbling here, falling there, getting up only to fall again — they reach the rank they desire; and once that is attained, we have seen many of them who, having passed through these Syrtes and Scyllas and Charybdises as though carried flying on the wings of favoring fortune — we have seen them, I say, ruling and governing the world from a chair, their hunger turned to plenty, their cold to comfort, their nakedness to fine clothing, their sleep on a mat to rest in holland sheets and damask: the justly earned reward of their virtue. But when set against and compared with what the warrior endures, everything they have endured falls far short of it, as I am now about to show."

title: Part 1, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Which deals with the remarkable speech Don Quixote gave on arms and letters

Continuing his speech, Don Quixote said: “Since we started with the student’s case — his poverty and everything that comes with it — let us now see whether the soldier is any richer. We will find that in poverty itself no one is poorer than he is, because he depends on his miserable pay, which arrives late or never, or else on whatever he can plunder, putting his life and his conscience in serious danger. Sometimes he is so close to naked that a slashed doublet has to serve him as both uniform and shirt, and in the dead of winter, out in the open field, he has nothing better to protect himself against the brutal weather than the breath of his own mouth — which, coming from an empty place, must come out cold, I hardly need to say, against all the laws of nature. True, he can look forward to nightfall to make up for all these discomforts in the bed that awaits him, a bed which — unless through some fault of his own — never sins by being too narrow, since he can measure out as much ground as he likes and roll around in it to his heart’s content without any fear of the sheets slipping off him. Then, after all this, suppose the day and hour arrive for him to take his degree in his profession — suppose the day of battle comes, when they fit him with his doctor’s cap made of lint, to patch some bullet hole, perhaps, that has gone through his temples or left him with a crippled arm or leg. And if that does not happen — if merciful Heaven watches over him and keeps him safe and sound — he may well find himself in the same poverty he was in before, and he will have to get through more engagements and more battles, and come out of every one victorious, before his situation improves; but miracles of that kind are rarely seen. Tell me, gentlemen, if you have ever thought about it: how far do the men who have profited from war fall short of the number of those who have died in it? You will surely answer that there is no comparison — that the dead cannot be counted, while the living who have been rewarded can be added up in three figures. It is the exact opposite for men of letters, because by their skirts — never mind their sleeves — they all find a way to support themselves; so although the soldier endures more, his reward is far smaller. Against all this you could argue that it is easier to reward two thousand soldiers, since the former can be paid with positions, which must necessarily go to men of their profession, while the latter can only be compensated out of the very property of the master they serve; but this impossibility only strengthens my argument.

“But let us set that aside, since it is a knotty question with no easy solution, and return to the superiority of arms over letters — a matter still unsettled, given how many arguments each side puts forward. Besides the ones I have already mentioned, letters claim that without them arms cannot sustain themselves, because war, too, has its laws and is governed by them, and laws fall within the territory of letters and of lettered men. To this, arms reply that without them laws cannot be upheld, because it is by arms that states are defended, kingdoms preserved, cities protected, roads kept safe, and seas cleared of pirates; in short, if it were not for arms, states, kingdoms, monarchies, cities, and the routes by sea and land would lie exposed to all the violence and chaos that war brings with it, for as long as it lasts and is free to use its privileges and powers. And it is obvious that whatever costs the most is valued, and deserves to be valued, the most. For a man to reach distinction in letters costs him time, sleepless nights, hunger, nakedness, headaches, indigestion, and other things of that kind, some of which I have already mentioned. But for a man to become a good soldier in the ordinary course of things costs him everything the student suffers, and to an incomparably higher degree, because at every step he runs the risk of losing his life. What fear of want or poverty that can reach or torment the student compares with what the soldier feels when he finds himself under siege in some stronghold, standing guard on some ravelin or cavalier, knowing that the enemy is digging a mine toward the post where he is stationed, and that under no circumstances can he withdraw or run from the imminent danger threatening him? All he can do is report what is happening to his captain, so that the captain can try to counter it with a counter-mine, and then hold his ground in dread, waiting for the moment when he will fly up to the clouds without wings and plunge into the depths against his will. And if that seems a trivial risk, consider whether it is matched or exceeded when two galleys ram each other head-on in the middle of the open sea, locked and tangled together, and the soldier has no more standing room than two feet of plank on the spur. Even though he sees in front of him as many ministers of death as the enemy has cannons pointed at him, barely a lance’s length from his body, and even though he knows that with the first careless step he will go down to visit the depths of Neptune’s bosom — still, with a fearless heart, driven on by the honor that steels him, he makes himself a target for all that musket fire and fights to cross that narrow path onto the enemy’s ship. And what is even more astonishing: no sooner has one man gone down into depths he will never rise from until the end of the world than another takes his place; and if he too falls into the sea that waits for him like an enemy, another follows, and then another, with not a moment’s pause between their deaths — the greatest courage and daring that all the fortunes of war can show. Happy were those blessed ages that never knew the dreadful fury of these devilish engines of artillery. Their inventor, I am convinced, is in hell, collecting the reward for his diabolical invention, which made it easy for a low, cowardly arm to take the life of a brave gentleman — so that, without his knowing how or from where, at the very height of the courage and fire that animate brave hearts, some random bullet arrives, fired perhaps by a man who fled in terror at the flash when he set off his accursed machine, and in an instant it ends the plans and cuts short the life of someone who deserved to live for ages to come. So when I think about this, I am almost tempted to say that in my heart I regret having taken up this profession of knight-errant in an age as detestable as the one we live in now; for though no danger can make me afraid, it still troubles me to think that powder and lead might rob me of the chance to make myself famous and renowned throughout the known world by the strength of my arm and the edge of my sword. But Heaven’s will be done. If I succeed in what I am attempting, I will be honored all the more, because I have faced greater dangers than the knights-errant of old ever exposed themselves to.”

Don Quixote delivered this whole lengthy speech while the others ate their supper, forgetting to lift a single bite to his lips, even though Sancho told him more than once to eat his meal, since he would have plenty of time afterward to say everything he wanted. Those who had heard him felt a fresh wave of pity at seeing a man who seemed perfectly sane, with sensible views on every subject he discussed, so hopelessly lost the moment his wretched, unlucky chivalry came into question. The curate told him he was entirely right in everything he had said in favor of arms, and that he himself, though a man of letters with a university degree, was of the same opinion.

They finished their supper and the table was cleared, and while the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes got Don Quixote of La Mancha’s garret ready — where it had been arranged that the women would sleep by themselves for the night — Don Fernando asked the captive to tell them the story of his life, since it was bound to be strange and absorbing, judging by the hints he had dropped when he arrived in Zoraida’s company. The captive replied that he would very gladly grant the request, though he feared the tale would not give them as much pleasure as he wished; still, rather than fail to oblige, he would tell it. The curate and the others thanked him and added their own pleas, and finding himself so pressed, he said there was no need to ask where a command carried such weight. “If you will give me your attention,” he added, “you will hear a true story that fictional ones, built with clever and studied art, may not be able to match.” These words made them settle into their places and keep a deep silence, and seeing them waiting on his words in silent expectation, he began in a calm, pleasant voice.

title: Part 1, Chapter 39
paragraphs: In which the captive tells the story of his life and adventures

My family came from a village in the mountains of Leon, and nature had treated it more kindly and generously than fortune ever did. Still, amid the general poverty of those communities, my father had a reputation as a rich man — and he really would have been one, if he had been as skilled at holding on to his property as he was at spending it. This habit of being open-handed and extravagant he had picked up from serving as a soldier in his youth, because the soldier's life is a school where the miser learns to be generous and the generous man learns to be a spendthrift; any soldiers who turn out to be misers are freaks you almost never see. My father went past generosity and edged into outright extravagance, a disposition that does no good at all to a married man with children who will inherit his name and position. My father had three children, all sons, and all old enough to choose a profession. Realizing, then, that he could not fight his own nature, he decided to strip himself of the very instrument and cause of his extravagance and waste — to strip himself of his wealth, without which Alexander the Great himself would have looked stingy. So one day he called the three of us aside into a room and spoke to us in words that went roughly like this:

"My sons, to convince you that I love you, nothing more needs to be known or said than that you are my sons; and to make you suspect that I do not love you, nothing more is needed than the knowledge that I have no self-control whatsoever when it comes to preserving your inheritance. So, to make sure that from now on you can trust that I love you like a father and have no desire to ruin you like a stepfather, I intend to do with you something I have been considering for a while and have settled on after careful deliberation. You are now old enough to choose your path in life, or at least to choose a calling that will bring you honor and profit when you are older. What I have decided to do is divide my property into four parts: three I will give to you, each receiving his portion with no favoritism, and the fourth I will keep to live on and support myself for whatever remains of the life Heaven chooses to grant me. But I want each of you, when he takes possession of the share that falls to him, to follow one of the paths I am about to lay out. In this Spain of ours there is a proverb that strikes me as very true — as they all are, being short sayings distilled from long practical experience — and the one I mean goes, 'The church, or the sea, or the king's house.' Put more plainly, it means: whoever wants to prosper and grow rich should either enter the church, or go to sea and take up commerce as his trade, or enter the king's service in his household, because as they say, 'Better a king's crumb than a lord's favor.' I say this because it is my will and my wish that one of you pursue learning, another business, and the third serve the king in his wars — for getting a place in his household service is hard to manage, and while war may not bring much wealth, it brings great distinction and fame. Eight days from now I will hand each of you his full share in cash, without cheating you of a single penny, as you will see in the end. Now tell me whether you are willing to follow my idea and my advice as I have set them out for you."

He called on me, as the eldest, to answer first. After urging him not to strip himself of his property but to spend all of it however he pleased — since we were young men perfectly capable of earning our own living — I agreed to go along with his wishes, and said that mine were to take up the profession of arms and through it serve God and my king. My second brother, after making the same plea, decided to go to the Indies, investing the portion that fell to him in trade. The youngest, and in my opinion the wisest, said he would rather enter the church, or go finish his studies at Salamanca. As soon as we had reached an understanding and chosen our professions, my father embraced us all, and within the short time he had named he carried out everything he had promised. When he had given each of us his share — which, as well as I remember, was three thousand ducats apiece in cash (an uncle of ours bought the estate and paid for it on the spot, so it would not pass out of the family) — all three of us said goodbye to our good father on the same day. And at that moment, since it seemed inhuman to me to leave my father with such meager resources in his old age, I persuaded him to take back two of my three thousand ducats, because the remainder would be enough to outfit me with everything a soldier needed. My two brothers, moved by my example, each gave him a thousand ducats, so my father was left with four thousand ducats in cash, plus another three thousand — the value of the portion that fell to him, which he preferred to keep as land rather than sell. Finally, as I said, we took our leave of him, and of the uncle I mentioned, not without sorrow and tears on both sides. They urged us to send word whenever we had the chance of how we were faring, whether well or badly. We promised we would, and when he had embraced us and given us his blessing, one of us set out for Salamanca, another for Seville, and I for Alicante, where I had heard a Genoese ship was loading a cargo of wool bound for Genoa.

It is now some twenty-two years since I left my father's house, and in all that time, though I have written several letters, I have had no news at all of him or of my brothers. As for my own adventures over that period, I will tell them briefly now. I sailed from Alicante, reached Genoa after a smooth voyage, and went on from there to Milan, where I equipped myself with weapons and a few pieces of a soldier's gear. From there I intended to go and enlist in Piedmont, but when I was already on the road to Alessandria della Paglia, I learned that the great Duke of Alva was on his way to Flanders. I changed my plans, joined him, served under him in the campaigns he fought, was present at the executions of the Counts Egmont and Horn, and rose to the rank of ensign under a famous captain from Guadalajara named Diego de Urbina. Some time after my arrival in Flanders, news came of the league that his Holiness Pope Pius V, of happy memory, had formed with Venice and Spain against the common enemy, the Turk, whose fleet had just captured the famous island of Cyprus, which belonged to the Venetians — a deplorable and disastrous loss. It was known for certain that the Most Serene Don John of Austria, natural brother of our good king Don Philip, was coming as commander-in-chief of the allied forces, and rumors were flying about the enormous preparations for war then underway. All of this stirred my heart and filled me with a longing to take part in the campaign everyone expected; and though I had reason to believe — and very nearly firm promises — that at the first opening I would be promoted to captain, I chose to leave everything behind and make my way, as I did, to Italy. As my luck would have it, Don John had just arrived at Genoa and was continuing on to Naples to join the Venetian fleet, which he later did at Messina. In short, I can say that I took part in that glorious expedition, by then promoted to captain of infantry — an honorable post my good luck, rather than my merits, raised me to. And on that day — so fortunate for Christendom, because on it every nation on earth was cured of the mistaken belief that the Turks were invincible at sea — on that day, I say, when Ottoman pride and arrogance were shattered, among all the men made happy there (for the Christians who died that day were happier than those who survived in victory) I alone was miserable. Instead of the naval crown I might have expected had it been Roman times, on the night that followed that famous day I found myself with shackles on my feet and manacles on my hands.

It happened like this. El Uchali, the king of Algiers, a bold and successful corsair, had attacked and captured the leading Maltese galley, leaving only three knights alive on board, all of them badly wounded. The flagship of John Andrea, which carried me and my company, came to its rescue, and doing what duty demands in such a situation, I leaped aboard the enemy galley. It then sheered away from the ship that had engaged it, which kept my men from following me, and so I found myself alone in the middle of my enemies — too many of them for me to resist. In short, I was captured, covered with wounds. El Uchali, as you know, gentlemen, escaped with his entire squadron, and I was left a prisoner in his hands, the one unhappy man among so many filled with joy, and the one captive among so many freed; for fifteen thousand Christians, all rowing at the oars of the Turkish fleet, regained their long-awaited liberty that day.

They took me to Constantinople, where the Grand Turk, Selim, made my master general at sea, because he had done his duty in the battle and had carried off the standard of the Order of Malta as proof of his bravery. The following year, which was the year seventy-two, I found myself at Navarino, rowing in the flagship with the three lanterns. There I saw, and noted, how the chance to capture the entire Turkish fleet in harbor was thrown away; for all the marines and janissaries on board were so sure they were about to be attacked inside the harbor itself that they had their kits and their pasamaques — their shoes — ready, so they could flee ashore at once without waiting for the assault, such was their terror of our fleet. But Heaven arranged things otherwise — not through any fault or negligence of the general commanding on our side, but because of the sins of Christendom, and because it is God's will and pleasure that we should always have instruments of punishment on hand to chastise us. As it turned out, El Uchali took refuge at Modon, which is an island near Navarino, and putting troops ashore, he fortified the mouth of the harbor and sat tight until Don John withdrew. On that expedition the galley called the Prize was captured, whose captain was a son of the famous corsair Barbarossa. It was taken by the chief Neapolitan galley called the She-wolf, commanded by that thunderbolt of war, that father to his men, that successful and undefeated captain Don Álvaro de Bazan, Marquis of Santa Cruz — and I cannot resist telling you what happened at the capture of the Prize.

The son of Barbarossa was so cruel, and treated his slaves so brutally, that when the men at the oars saw the She-wolf galley bearing down on them and closing the distance, they all dropped their oars at once and seized their captain, who was standing on the platform at the end of the gangway, screaming at them to row harder. Passing him along from bench to bench, from the stern to the bow, they bit him so savagely that before he had been carried much past the mast his soul had already gone to hell — so great, as I said, was the cruelty with which he treated them, and the hatred with which they hated him.

We returned to Constantinople, and the following year, seventy-three, word spread that Don John had seized Tunis, taken the kingdom from the Turks, and installed Muley Hamet in power — ending the hopes that Muley Hamida, the cruelest and bravest Moor in the world, had nursed of returning to rule there. The Grand Turk took the loss bitterly to heart, and with the cunning his whole race possesses, he made peace with the Venetians (who wanted it far more eagerly than he did), and the following year, seventy-four, he attacked the Goletta and the fort that Don John had left half built near Tunis. Through all these events I was laboring at the oar with no hope of freedom; at least I had no hope of winning it by ransom, because I was firmly determined not to write to my father and tell him of my misfortunes. In the end the Goletta fell, and the fort fell too. Arrayed against those positions were seventy-five thousand regular Turkish soldiers, plus more than four hundred thousand Moors and Arabs from every part of Africa, and trailing behind that enormous host came such munitions and engines of war, and so many sappers, that with their bare hands they could have buried the Goletta and the fort under handfuls of earth. The Goletta, until then considered impregnable, fell first — and it fell through no fault of its defenders, who did everything they could and should have done, but because experience proved how easily trenches could be dug in the desert sand there. Water used to be found at a depth of two palms, while the Turks found none at two yards; and so, using a great quantity of sandbags, they raised their earthworks so high that they overlooked the walls of the fort, sweeping them with fire as if from a raised battery, so that no one could make a stand or keep up the defense.

It was a common opinion that our men should not have shut themselves up inside the Goletta but should have waited in the open at the landing place; but those who say so are talking carelessly, with little understanding of such matters. If the Goletta and the fort together held barely seven thousand soldiers, how could so small a force, however determined, march out and hold its ground against enemy numbers like those? And how can anyone avoid losing a stronghold that receives no relief, especially when it is surrounded by a host of determined enemies fighting on their own soil? But many believed — and I believed it too — that it was a special favor and mercy that Heaven showed Spain in allowing the destruction of that breeding ground and hiding place of trouble, that devourer, that sponge, that moth of endless money, wasted there fruitlessly for no purpose except preserving the memory of its capture by the invincible Charles V — as if those stones were needed to make that memory eternal, which it is and always will be. The fort fell too, but the Turks had to win it inch by inch, because the soldiers defending it fought so bravely and stubbornly that the enemy dead in twenty-two general assaults came to more than twenty-five thousand. Of the three hundred defenders who survived, not one was taken without wounds — clear and unmistakable proof of their courage and resolve, and of how sturdily they had defended themselves and held their post. A small fort, or tower, that stood in the middle of the lagoon under the command of Don Juan Zanoguera, a Valencian gentleman and a famous soldier, surrendered on terms. They took prisoner Don Pedro Puertocarrero, commandant of the Goletta, who had done everything in his power to defend his fortress and felt its loss so deeply that he died of grief on the road to Constantinople, where they were carrying him as a prisoner. They also captured the commandant of the fort, a man named Gabrio Cerbellon, a Milanese gentleman, a great engineer and a very brave soldier. Many notable people died in those two fortresses, among them Pagano Doria, a knight of the Order of St. John and a man of generous character, as he showed by his extraordinary openhandedness toward his brother, the famous John Andrea Doria. What made his death sadder still was that he was killed by some Arabs to whom, once he saw the fort was lost, he had entrusted himself, and who had offered to guide him, disguised as a Moor, to Tabarca, a small fort or trading post on the coast held by the Genoese who worked the coral fishery. Those Arabs cut off his head and carried it to the commander of the Turkish fleet, who demonstrated on them the truth of our Castilian proverb that "though the treason may please, the traitor is hated" — for they say he ordered the men who brought him the gift to be hanged for not having brought Doria alive.

Among the Christians captured in the fort was a man named Don Pedro de Aguilar, a native of some town in Andalusia — I do not know which — who had served as ensign in the fort, a soldier of high reputation and rare intelligence, and one who had, in particular, a special gift for what they call poetry. I mention this because his fate brought him to my galley and to my bench, and made him a slave to the same master; and before we left the port this gentleman composed two sonnets as epitaphs, one on the Goletta and the other on the fort. In fact, I might as well recite them, because I know them by heart, and I think they will please rather than displease.

The instant the captive mentioned the name Don Pedro de Aguilar, Don Fernando glanced at his companions, and all three of them smiled; and when he came to the subject of the sonnets, one of them said, "Before your worship goes any further, I beg you to tell me what became of that Don Pedro de Aguilar you have been speaking of."

"All I know," the captive replied, "is that after spending two years in Constantinople, he escaped disguised as an Arnaut, in the company of a Greek spy; but whether he regained his freedom or not, I cannot say — though I suspect he did, because a year later I saw the Greek in Constantinople, but I had no chance to ask him how the journey had turned out."
"Well, you are right," the gentleman answered, "because that Don Pedro is my brother, and he is in our village right now, in good health — rich, married, and the father of three children."
"Thanks be to God for all the mercies he has shown him," said the captive, "because in my opinion there is no happiness on earth that compares with recovering one's lost liberty."
"And what is more," said the gentleman, "I know the sonnets my brother wrote."
"Then let your worship recite them," said the captive, "because you will deliver them better than I could."
"Gladly, with all my heart," said the gentleman. "The one on the Goletta goes like this."

title: Part 1, Chapter 40
paragraphs: In which the captive's story continues
SONNET

"Blessed souls, set free from this mortal husk, rewarded for brave deeds and exalted, you now dwell above this lowly globe of ours, made heirs of heaven and immortality. With noble rage and burning ardour, while your strength was yours, you plied it in battle, and with your own blood and the enemy's stained the sandy soil and the encircling sea. It was the ebbing life-blood that failed your weary arms first; the stout hearts never quailed. Though defeated, you still earned the victor's crown: though mourned, your fall was still a triumph, for there, between sword and wall, you won glory in heaven and renown on earth."
"That is exactly it, as I recall," said the captive.
"Well then, the one about the fort," said the gentleman, "if my memory serves me, goes like this:"
SONNET

"Up from this wasted soil, this shattered shell, whose walls and towers lie here in ruin, three thousand soldier souls took wing on high to dwell in the bright mansions of the blessed. They tried in vain, with all the strength of their arms, to repel the enemy's onslaught, and when at last nothing remained but to die, the last defenders fell, wearied and few. And this same arid soil has always been the haunt of countless mournful memories, as much in our day as in days of old. But never yet, I think, has it sent to heaven from its hard bosom purer souls than these, or borne braver bodies on its surface."
The sonnets were not disliked, and the captive was glad of the news they gave him of his comrade. Continuing his tale, he went on:

With La Goletta and the fort now in their hands, the Turks gave orders to dismantle La Goletta — the fort was reduced to such a state that there was nothing left to level — and to do the work faster they mined it in three places. But nowhere were they able to blow up what seemed the weakest part, that is, the old walls, while everything left standing of the new fortifications the Fratin had built came down with the greatest ease. Eventually the fleet returned victorious and triumphant to Constantinople, and a few months later my master, El Uchali — otherwise Uchali Fartax, which in Turkish means "the scabby renegade" — died. He certainly was scabby; it is the Turks' custom to name people from some defect or virtue they possess, the reason being that among them there are only four surnames belonging to families tracing descent from the Ottoman house, and the rest, as I said, take their names and surnames from either bodily blemishes or moral qualities. This "scabby one" rowed at the oar as a slave of the Grand Signor's for fourteen years, and when he was past thirty-four, in resentment at having been struck by a Turk at the oar, he turned renegade and renounced his faith in order to take his revenge. And such was his valour that, without rising by the base methods most of the Grand Signor's favourites use, he came to be king of Algiers and afterwards general at sea, which is the third position of trust in the realm. He was a Calabrian by birth and a worthy man morally, and he treated his slaves with great humanity. He had three thousand of them, and after his death they were divided, as he directed in his will, between the Grand Signor (who is heir of all who die, sharing with the dead man's children) and his renegades. I fell to the lot of a Venetian renegade who, as a cabin boy on a ship, had been captured by Uchali and was so loved by him that he became one of his most favoured boys. He turned into the cruellest renegade I ever saw: his name was Hassan Aga, and he grew very rich and became king of Algiers. With him I went there from Constantinople, rather glad to be so much nearer Spain — not that I planned to write to anyone about my unhappy lot, but to try whether fortune would be kinder to me in Algiers than in Constantinople, where I had tried in a thousand ways to escape without ever finding the right moment or chance. In Algiers I resolved to look for other means of carrying out the purpose I cherished so dearly, for the hope of regaining my liberty never deserted me. When my plots and schemes and attempts did not turn out as I expected, instead of giving way to despair I would immediately look for or invent some new hope to keep me going, however faint or feeble it might be.

In this way I went on living, shut up in a building or prison the Turks call a baño, where they confine their Christian captives — those of the king's, those of private owners, and those they call "of the Almacen," meaning slaves of the municipality, who work on the city's public works and other jobs. Captives of this last kind recover their liberty only with great difficulty, because, being public property and having no particular master, there is no one to negotiate ransom with even if they have the means. To these baños, as I said, certain private individuals of the town are in the habit of bringing their captives, especially when they are being held for ransom, because there they can keep them safely and comfortably until the ransom arrives. The king's captives held for ransom likewise do not go out to work with the rest of the crew, unless their ransom is delayed; then, to make them write more urgently, they are forced to work and gather wood, which is no light labour.

I, however, was one of those held for ransom, because when it was discovered that I was a captain, although I declared my meagre means and lack of fortune, nothing would persuade them not to count me among the gentlemen and those awaiting ransom. They put a chain on me, more as a mark of this than for safekeeping, and so I passed my life in that baño with several other gentlemen and persons of quality singled out as held for ransom. Although at times — or rather almost always — we suffered from hunger and inadequate clothing, nothing distressed us so much as seeing and hearing at every turn the unparalleled and unheard-of cruelties my master inflicted on the Christians. Every day he hanged a man, impaled another, cut off someone's ears — all with so little provocation, or with none at all, that even the Turks acknowledged he did it just for the sake of doing it, since he was by nature murderously disposed towards the entire human race. The only one who fared at all well with him was a Spanish soldier, someone de Saavedra by name, to whom he never gave a blow himself or ordered one given, or addressed a harsh word, although he had done things that will dwell in the memory of the people there for many a year — all to recover his liberty. For the least of the many things he did, we all dreaded he would be impaled, and he himself feared it more than once; and only because time does not allow, I could tell you now things that soldier did which would interest and astonish you far more than the narration of my own tale.

To go on with my story: the courtyard of our prison was overlooked by the windows of the house of a wealthy Moor of high position. As is usual in Moorish houses, these were loopholes rather than windows, and besides were covered with thick, close lattice-work. It happened, then, that one day I was on the terrace of our prison with three other comrades, passing the time by seeing how far we could leap with our chains. We were alone, all the other Christians having gone out to work. I happened to raise my eyes, and from one of those little closed windows I saw a reed appear with a cloth attached to the end of it, and it kept waving and moving as if making signs to us to come and take it. We watched it, and one of those with me went and stood under the reed to see whether they would drop it or what they would do, but as he did so the reed was raised and moved from side to side, as if saying "no" by a shake of the head. The Christian came back, and the reed was lowered again, making the same movements as before. Another of my comrades went, and the same thing happened to him as to the first, and then the third went forward, with the same result. Seeing this I did not want to miss my own chance, and as soon as I came under the reed it was dropped and fell inside the baño at my feet. I hurried to untie the cloth, in which I noticed a knot, and inside it were ten cianis, which are coins of base gold current among the Moors, each worth ten reals of our money.

Needless to say I rejoiced over this windfall, and my joy was matched by my wonder as I tried to imagine how this good fortune could have come to us, and especially to me — for the evident unwillingness to drop the reed for anyone but me showed that the favour was intended for me. I took my welcome money, broke the reed, and returned to the terrace. Looking up at the window, I saw a very white hand put out, which opened and shut very quickly. From this we gathered, or imagined, that it must be some woman living in that house who had done us this kindness, and to show that we were grateful we made salaams in the Moorish fashion, bowing the head, bending the body, and crossing our arms on our chest. Shortly afterwards, at the same window, a small cross made of reeds was put out and immediately withdrawn. This sign led us to believe that some Christian woman was a captive in the house, and that it was she who had been so kind to us; but the whiteness of the hand and the bracelets we had glimpsed made us dismiss that idea. We thought instead that it might be one of those Christian renegades whom their masters often take as lawful wives, and gladly, since they prefer them to the women of their own nation. In all our guesses we were wide of the truth. From then on our sole occupation was watching and gazing at the window where the cross had appeared, as if it were our pole-star. But at least fifteen days passed without our seeing either it, or the hand, or any other sign. Meanwhile, though we tried with all our might to find out who lived in the house, and whether there was any Christian renegade in it, no one could tell us anything more than that the man living there was a rich Moor of high position called Hadji Morato, formerly alcaide of La Pata, an office of high dignity among them. But when we least expected any more cianis to rain from that quarter, we suddenly saw the reed appear again, this time with another cloth tied in a larger knot, and this at a moment when, as before, the baño was deserted and empty.

We tried as before, the same three going forward before me; but the reed was delivered to no one but me, and on my approach it was let drop. I untied the knot and found forty Spanish gold crowns and a paper written in Arabic, with a large cross drawn at the end. I kissed the cross, took the crowns, and returned to the terrace, and we all made our salaams. The hand appeared again, I signed that I would read the paper, and then the window was closed. We were all puzzled but filled with joy at what had taken place; and since none of us understood Arabic, our curiosity to know what the paper contained was great, and the difficulty of finding someone to read it even greater. At last I decided to confide in a renegade, a native of Murcia, who professed great friendship for me and had given pledges binding him to keep any secret I might entrust to him. It is the practice with some renegades, when they intend to return to Christian territory, to carry around certificates from notable captives stating, in whatever form they can, that such-and-such a renegade is a worthy man who has always shown kindness to Christians and is eager to escape on the first opportunity. Some obtain these testimonials with good intentions, others put them to cunning use: when they go raiding on Christian territory, if they are wrecked or captured they produce their certificates and say that these papers show why they came — to remain on Christian ground — and that this is why they had joined the Turks in their raid. By this means they escape the consequences of the first outburst and make peace with the Church before it does them any harm, and then, when they have the chance, they return to Barbary to become what they were before. Others, however, do procure these papers and use them honestly, and remain on Christian soil. This friend of mine was one of those renegades I have described: he had certificates from all our comrades, in which we testified for him as strongly as we could; and if the Moors had found the papers they would have burned him alive.

I knew he understood Arabic very well, and could not only speak but also write it; but before I disclosed the whole matter to him, I asked him to read for me this paper which I had, I said, found by accident in a hole in my cell. He opened it and spent some time examining it and muttering to himself as he translated. I asked him whether he understood it, and he said he did perfectly, and that if I wanted him to tell me its meaning word for word, I must give him pen and ink so that he could do it properly. We at once gave him what he asked for, and he set about translating it bit by bit. When he had finished he said:
"All that is here in Spanish is what the Moorish paper contains, and you must remember that when it says 'Lela Marien' it means 'Our Lady the Virgin Mary.'"
We read the paper, and it ran like this:

"When I was a child my father had a slave who taught me to say the Christian prayer in my own language, and told me many things about Lela Marien. The Christian woman died, and I know she did not go to the fire but to Allah, because since then I have seen her twice, and she told me to go to the land of the Christians to see Lela Marien, who has great love for me. I do not know how to go. I have seen many Christians, but except for you none has seemed to me a gentleman. I am young and beautiful, and have plenty of money to bring with me. See if you can contrive how we may go, and if you wish you shall be my husband there, and if not it will not distress me, because Lela Marien will find me someone to marry me. I myself have written this: take care to whom you give it to read; trust no Moor, for they are all treacherous. I am greatly troubled about this, because I would not have you confide in anyone — if my father knew of it he would at once throw me down a well and cover me with stones. I will tie a thread to the reed; fasten the answer to it, and if you have no one to write for you in Arabic, tell it to me by signs, for Lela Marien will make me understand you. May she and Allah and this cross, which I often kiss as the captive woman told me to, protect you."

Judge, sirs, whether we had reason to feel surprise and joy at the words of this paper. Both were so great that the renegade realised the paper had not been found by chance but had really been addressed to one of us; and he begged us, if his suspicion was correct, to trust him and tell him everything, because he would risk his life for our freedom. So saying, he took from his breast a metal crucifix and, with many tears, swore by the God it represented — in whom, sinful and wicked as he was, he truly and faithfully believed — to be loyal to us and to keep secret whatever we chose to reveal to him; for he thought, and almost foresaw, that through the woman who had written that paper he and all of us would obtain our liberty, and he himself would obtain what he so much desired, his restoration to the bosom of Holy Mother Church, from which by his own sin and ignorance he was now severed like a corrupt limb. The renegade said this with so many tears and such signs of repentance that we all agreed unanimously to tell him the whole truth, and so we gave him a full account, hiding nothing. We pointed out the window at which the reed had appeared, and by this means he took note of the house and resolved to find out with particular care who lived in it. We also agreed it would be wise to answer the Moorish lady's letter, and the renegade, without a moment's delay, took down the words I dictated, which were exactly what I shall tell you — for nothing of importance in this affair has escaped my memory, or ever will while life lasts. This, then, was the answer sent back to the Moorish lady:

"May the true Allah protect you, Lady, and that blessed Marien who is the true mother of God, and who has put it in your heart to go to the land of the Christians, because she loves you. Beg her to be pleased to show you how you can carry out what she commands, for she will, such is her goodness. On my part, and on the part of all these Christians with me, I promise to do all we can for you, even to death. Do not fail to write to me and tell me what you mean to do, and I will always answer; for the great Allah has given us a Christian captive who can speak and write your language well, as you can see from this paper. So without fear you can tell us anything you wish. As to your saying that if you reach the land of the Christians you will be my wife, I give you my promise on it as a good Christian; and know that Christians keep their promises better than the Moors do. May Allah and Marien his mother watch over you, my Lady."

With the paper written and folded, I waited two days until the baño was empty as before, and immediately took my usual walk on the terrace to see if there was any sign of the reed, which was not long in appearing. As soon as I saw it, although I could not make out who was holding it, I showed the paper as a sign to attach the thread; but the thread was already fixed to the reed, and to it I tied the paper. Shortly afterwards our star once more appeared with the white flag of peace — the little bundle. It was dropped, I picked it up, and found in the cloth, in gold and silver coins of all sorts, more than fifty crowns, which fifty times over strengthened our joy and doubled our hope of gaining our liberty. That very night our renegade returned and said he had learned that the Moor we had been told of did live in that house, that his name was Hadji Morato, that he was enormously rich, that he had one only daughter who was heiress to all his wealth, and that it was the general opinion throughout the city that she was the most beautiful woman in Barbary. Several of the viceroys who came there had sought her in marriage, but she had always been unwilling to marry. He had also learned that she had had a Christian slave woman who was now dead — all of which agreed with the contents of the paper. We immediately took counsel with the renegade about what means we should use to carry off the Moorish lady and bring us all to Christian territory. In the end it was agreed that for the present we should wait for a second message from Zoraida (that was the name of the woman who now wishes to be called Maria), because we saw clearly that she, and no one else, could find a way out of all these difficulties. Once we had decided this, the renegade told us not to worry, that he would either lose his life or restore us to liberty. For four days the baño was crowded with people, so the reed delayed its appearance for four days; but at the end of that time, when the baño was as usual empty, the reed reappeared with a cloth so bulky it promised a happy birth. Reed and cloth came down to me, and I found another paper and a hundred crowns in gold, with no other coin. The renegade was present, and in our cell we gave him the paper to read, which ran as follows:

"I cannot think of a plan, señor, for our going to Spain, nor has Lela Marien shown me one, though I have asked her. All that can be done is for me to give you plenty of gold from this window. Use it to ransom yourself and your friends, and let one of you go to the land of the Christians, buy a vessel there, and come back for the others. He will find me in my father's garden, which is at the Babazon gate near the seashore, where I shall be all this summer with my father and my servants. You can carry me away from there by night without any danger and bring me to the vessel. And remember you are to be my husband, or else I will pray to Marien to punish you. If you cannot trust anyone to go for the vessel, ransom yourself and you go, because I know you will return more surely than any other, since you are a gentleman and a Christian. Try to acquaint yourself with the garden; and when I see you walking out there, I shall know the baño is empty and I will give you plenty of money. Allah protect you, señor."

These were the words and contents of the second paper, and on hearing them each man declared himself willing to be the one ransomed and promised to go and return in scrupulous good faith. I made the same offer too. But the renegade objected to all this, saying he would on no account agree to one being set free before all went together, as experience had taught him how badly those who were set free kept the promises they had made in captivity. Captives of distinction frequently used this trick, he said, paying the ransom of one who was to go to Valencia or Majorca with money to fit out a bark and return for the others who had ransomed him — only never to come back; for recovered liberty, and the dread of losing it again, wipe from the memory every obligation in the world. To prove what he said, he told us briefly what had happened to a certain Christian gentleman almost at that very time — the strangest case that had ever occurred even there, where astonishing and marvellous things happen every moment. In short, he ended by saying that what could and ought to be done was for us to give him the money intended for the ransom of one of us Christians, so that he could buy a vessel in Algiers under the pretext of becoming a merchant trading at Tetuan and along the coast. As master of the vessel it would be easy for him to find some way of getting us all out of the baño and on board, especially if the Moorish lady gave, as she said, enough money to ransom us all — because once free it would be the simplest thing in the world for us to embark even in broad daylight. But the great difficulty was that the Moors do not allow any renegade to buy or own any craft, unless it be a large vessel for raiding expeditions, because they fear that anyone who buys a small vessel, especially a Spaniard, only wants it to escape to Christian territory. He could get around this, however, by arranging with a Tagarin Moor to share with him in buying the vessel and in the profit on the cargo. Under this cover he could become master of the vessel, in which case he considered all the rest as good as done. Now, although my comrades and I thought it would be a better plan to send to Majorca for the vessel, as the Moorish lady suggested, we did not dare oppose him, fearing that if we did not do as he said he would denounce us and put us all in danger of losing our lives, if he revealed our dealings with Zoraida, for whose life we would have all given our own. So we resolved to put ourselves in the hands of God and in the renegade's; and at the same time an answer was sent to Zoraida, telling her we would do everything she advised, since she had given us as good counsel as if Lela Marien had spoken it, and that it depended on her alone whether we deferred the business or carried it out at once. I renewed my promise to be her husband; and so, the next day the baño chanced to be empty, she gave us at different times, by means of the reed and cloth, two thousand gold crowns and a paper saying that the next Juma — that is, Friday — she was going to her father's garden, but that before she went she would give us more money. If it was not enough we were to let her know, and she would give us as much as we asked, because her father had so much he would not miss it, and besides she kept all the keys.

We at once gave the renegade five hundred crowns to buy the vessel, and with eight hundred I ransomed myself, giving the money to a Valencian merchant who happened to be in Algiers at the time. He had me released on his word, pledging that on the arrival of the first ship from Valencia he would pay my ransom; for if he had handed over the money at once it would have made the king suspect that my ransom money had been in Algiers for a long time, and that the merchant had kept it secret for his own gain. In fact my master was so hard to deal with that I dared not on any account pay the money down at once. The Thursday before the Friday on which the fair Zoraida was to go to the garden, she gave us another thousand crowns and warned us of her departure, begging me, if I were ransomed, to find out her father's garden at once and to seek every opportunity of going there to see her. I answered briefly that I would do so, and that she must remember to commend us to Lela Marien with all the prayers the captive woman had taught her. This done, steps were taken to ransom our three comrades, so as to get them out of the baño; for otherwise, seeing me ransomed and themselves not, even though the money was forthcoming, they might make a fuss about it, and the devil might prompt them to do something that would harm Zoraida. Although their station might have been enough to relieve me of this fear, I was unwilling to take any risk in the matter, and so I had them ransomed in the same way I was, handing over all the money to the merchant so that he could give security with safety and confidence — without, however, confiding our arrangement and secret to him, which might have been dangerous.

title: Part 1, Chapter 41
paragraphs: In which the captive continues his adventures

Before fifteen days were up our renegade had already purchased an excellent vessel with room for more than thirty people. To make the transaction safe and give it cover, he thought it best to make, as he did, a voyage to a place called Shershel, twenty leagues from Algiers on the Oran side, where there is an extensive trade in dried figs. He made this voyage two or three times in company with the Tagarin already mentioned. (The Moors of Aragon are called Tagarins in Barbary, and those of Granada Mudéjares; but in the Kingdom of Fez they call the Mudéjares Elches, and they are the people the king mostly employs in war.) Each time he passed with his vessel he anchored in a cove not two crossbow shots from the garden where Zoraida was waiting. There the renegade, together with the two Moorish lads who rowed, used to station himself on purpose, either saying his prayers or rehearsing what he meant to do for real. He would also go to Zoraida's garden and ask for fruit, which her father gave him, not knowing him. But although, as he afterwards told me, he tried to speak to Zoraida and tell her who he was, and that by my orders he was to take her to the land of the Christians so she might feel reassured, he had never been able to: Moorish women do not allow themselves to be seen by any Moor or Turk unless their husband or father bids them; with Christian captives they permit freedom of intercourse and communication, even more than might be considered proper. For my part I would have been sorry if he had spoken to her, since it might have alarmed her to find her affairs being discussed by renegades. But God, who ordered things otherwise, gave our renegade no opportunity for his well-meant attempt. Seeing how safely he could go to Shershel and back, anchoring when and where and how he liked, and that the Tagarin his partner had no will but his — and now that I was ransomed, all we needed was to find some Christians to row — he told me to look out for any I would be willing to take with me, beyond those who had been ransomed, and to engage them for the next Friday, which he had set for our departure. So I spoke to twelve Spaniards, all stout rowers and the sort who could most easily slip out of the city; but it was no easy matter to find that many just then, because there were twenty ships out cruising and they had taken all the rowers with them. These would not have been found if it had not been that their master had stayed at home that summer without going to sea, in order to finish a galliot he had on the stocks. I said nothing more to these men than that the next Friday in the evening they were to come out stealthily one by one and hang about Hadji Morato's garden, waiting for me until I came. I gave each one these directions separately, with orders that if they saw any other Christians there, they were to say nothing to them except that I had directed them to wait at that spot.

With this preliminary settled, another, still more necessary step had to be taken: to let Zoraida know how matters stood, so that she might be prepared and not be taken by surprise if we were suddenly to seize her before she thought the Christians' vessel could have returned. I decided, therefore, to go to the garden and try to speak to her. The day before my departure I went there on the pretext of gathering herbs. The first person I met was her father, who addressed me in the language that all over Barbary and even in Constantinople serves as the medium between captives and Moors — neither Morisco nor Castilian, nor of any other nation, but a mixture of all languages by which we can all understand one another. In this sort of language, I say, he asked me what I wanted in his garden and to whom I belonged. I replied that I was a slave of the Arnaut Mami (I knew for a certainty that this man was a great friend of his), and that I wanted some herbs to make a salad. He then asked me whether I was being held for ransom and what my master was asking for me. While these questions and answers were going on, the fair Zoraida, who had spotted me some time before, came out of the house in the garden; and as Moorish women are by no means particular about being seen by Christians, or, as I said before, at all coy, she had no hesitation in coming over to where her father was standing with me. Moreover her father, seeing her approach slowly, called her to come. It would be beyond me to describe now the great beauty, the high-bred air, the brilliant attire of my beloved Zoraida as she presented herself before my eyes. I will content myself with saying that more pearls hung from her fair neck, her ears, and her hair than she had hairs on her head. On her ankles — which, as is customary, were bare — she had carcajes (which is the Morisco word for bracelets or anklets) of the purest gold, set with so many diamonds that, she told me afterwards, her father valued them at ten thousand doubloons, and those on her wrists were worth as much again. The pearls were abundant and very fine, since the highest display and adornment of Moorish women is to deck themselves with rich pearls and seed-pearls; and so there are more such pearls among the Moors than among any other people. Zoraida's father had the reputation of owning a great number, and the purest in all Algiers, and also of having more than two hundred thousand Spanish crowns; and she, who is now mistress of me alone, was mistress of all that. Whether thus adorned she would have been beautiful or not, and what she must have been in her prosperity, may be imagined from the beauty that remains to her after so many hardships.
