As everyone knows, the beauty of some women has its times and its seasons, increased or diminished by chance causes; and naturally the emotions of the mind heighten or impair it, though more often they completely destroy it. In a word, she presented herself before me that day attired with the utmost splendour, and supremely beautiful — at any rate, she seemed to me the most beautiful thing I had ever seen; and when I added to that everything I owed her, I felt as though I had before me some heavenly being come to earth to bring me relief and happiness.
As she came over her father told her in his own language that I was a captive belonging to his friend the Arnaut Mami, and that I had come for salad.
She took up the conversation, and in that mixture of tongues I have spoken of she asked me if I was a gentleman, and why I was not ransomed.

I answered that I was already ransomed, and that the price showed what value my master set on me, since they had been paid one thousand five hundred zoltanis for me. To which she replied, "If you had been my father's, I tell you I would not have let him part with you for twice as much, because you Christians always tell lies about yourselves and make yourselves out poor to cheat the Moors."
"That may be, lady," I said; "but I really did deal truthfully with my master, as I do and mean to do with everybody in the world."
"And when do you go?" said Zoraida.
"Tomorrow, I think," I said, "because there is a vessel here from France that sails tomorrow, and I think I shall go in her."
"Would it not be better," said Zoraida, "to wait for the arrival of ships from Spain and go with them, and not with the French, who are not your friends?"

"No," I said; "though if there were word that a Spanish ship was now coming, it is true I might perhaps wait for it. But it is more likely I shall leave tomorrow, because the longing I feel to return to my country and to those I love is so strong that it will not let me wait for another opportunity, however better, if it is delayed."
"No doubt you are married in your own country," said Zoraida, "and so you are anxious to go and see your wife."
"I am not married," I replied, "but I have given my promise to marry when I arrive there."
"And is the lady to whom you have given it beautiful?" said Zoraida.
"So beautiful," I said, "that to describe her properly and tell you the truth, she is very like you."

At this her father laughed very heartily and said, "By Allah, Christian, she must be very beautiful if she is like my daughter, who is the most beautiful woman in all this kingdom. Just look at her well, and you will see I am telling the truth."

Zoraida's father, as the better linguist, helped interpret most of these words and phrases, because although she spoke that bastard language used there, she expressed her meaning more by signs than by words.

While we were still engaged in this conversation, a Moor came running up shouting that four Turks had leaped over the fence or wall of the garden and were gathering the fruit, even though it was not yet ripe. The old man was alarmed and Zoraida too, for the Moors commonly — almost instinctively — dread the Turks, but particularly the soldiers, who are so insolent and domineering to the Moors under their power that they treat them worse than if they were their slaves. Her father said to Zoraida, "Daughter, go into the house and shut yourself in while I go and speak to these dogs. And you, Christian, pick your herbs and go in peace, and may Allah bring you safe to your own country."

I bowed, and he went off to look for the Turks, leaving me alone with Zoraida, who pretended to be about to retire as her father had told her. But the moment he was hidden by the trees of the garden, she turned to me with her eyes full of tears and said, "Tameji, cristiano, tameji?" — that is, "Are you going, Christian, are you going?"
I answered, "Yes, lady, but not without you, come what may. Watch out for me on the next Juma, and don't be alarmed when you see us, for we shall most certainly go to the land of the Christians."

I said this in such a way that she perfectly understood everything that had passed between us. Throwing her arm round my neck, she began with feeble steps to move towards the house; but as fate would have it (and it might have gone very badly if heaven had not otherwise ordered it), just as we were moving on in the manner and position I have described, with her arm round my neck, her father, returning after having sent the Turks away, saw how we were walking, and we saw that he saw us. But Zoraida, ready and quick-witted, did not take her arm from my neck — on the contrary, she drew closer to me and laid her head on my breast, bending her knees a little and showing every sign of fainting, while I at the same time made it look as though I were supporting her against my will. Her father came running up to where we were, and seeing his daughter in this state asked what was the matter with her. Since she gave no answer, he said, "No doubt she has fainted in alarm at the entrance of those dogs," and taking her from me he drew her to his own breast, while she, sighing, her eyes still wet with tears, said again, "Ameji, cristiano, ameji" — "Go, Christian, go." To which her father replied, "There is no need, daughter, for the Christian to go, because he has done you no harm, and the Turks have now gone. Do not be alarmed, there is nothing to hurt you, for, as I say, the Turks at my request have gone back the way they came."

"It was they who terrified her, as you said, señor," I said to her father; "but since she tells me to go, I have no wish to displease her. Peace be with you, and with your leave I will come back to this garden for herbs if need be, because my master says nowhere are there better herbs for salad than here."

"Come back for any you need," replied Hadji Morato, "for my daughter does not speak this way because she is displeased with you or with any Christian. She only meant that the Turks should go, not you; or that it was time for you to look for your herbs."

With this I at once took my leave of both, and she, looking as though her heart were breaking, withdrew with her father. While pretending to look for herbs I made my way around the garden at my ease, studying carefully all the approaches and exits, and the fastenings of the house, and everything that could be used to make our task easier.

Having done so, I went and gave an account of all that had happened to the renegade and my comrades, and looked forward impatiently to the hour when, all fear at an end, I should find myself in possession of the prize fortune was holding out to me in the fair and lovely Zoraida. The time passed at last, and the appointed day we so longed for arrived; and, all following the arrangement and plan we had decided on after careful consideration and many long discussions, we succeeded as fully as we could have wished. On the Friday following the day on which I had spoken to Zoraida in the garden, the renegade anchored his vessel at nightfall almost opposite the spot where she was. The Christians who were to row were ready and hiding in different places round about, all waiting for me, anxious and elated, eager to attack the vessel they had before their eyes; for they did not know the renegade's plan and expected to gain their liberty by force of arms and by killing the Moors on board the vessel. As soon, then, as I and my comrades made our appearance, all those in hiding saw us and came to join us. By now it was the time when the city gates are shut, and no one was to be seen in all the space outside. Once we were gathered together, we debated whether it would be better first to go for Zoraida or to take the Moorish rowers prisoner on the vessel; but while we were still undecided our renegade came up asking what was keeping us, since it was now the time and all the Moors were off their guard, most of them asleep. We told him why we were hesitating, but he said it was more important first to secure the vessel, which could be done with the greatest ease and without any danger, and then we could go for Zoraida. We all approved of what he said, and so without further delay, with him as our guide, we made for the vessel. He leaped on board first, drew his cutlass, and said in Morisco, "Let no one stir from here unless he wants it to cost him his life." By this time almost all the Christians were on board, and the Moors, who were fainthearted, hearing their captain speak this way were cowed; and without one of them taking up arms (and they had few or hardly any), they submitted without a word to being bound by the Christians, who quickly secured them, warning them that if they raised any kind of outcry they would all be put to the sword. With this accomplished, and half of our party left to keep guard over them, the rest of us, again taking the renegade as our guide, hurried to Hadji Morato's garden. As good luck would have it, on trying the gate it opened as easily as if it had not been locked; and so, quietly and in silence, we reached the house without being noticed by anyone. The lovely Zoraida was watching for us at a window, and as soon as she saw there were people there she asked in a low voice if we were "Nizarani," meaning to ask if we were Christians. I answered that we were, and begged her to come down. As soon as she recognised me she did not delay an instant, but without answering a word came down immediately, opened the door, and presented herself before us all, so beautiful and so richly attired that I cannot attempt to describe her. The moment I saw her I took her hand and kissed it, and the renegade and my two comrades did the same; and the rest, who knew nothing of the circumstances, did as they saw us do, since it only looked as if we were thanking her and recognising her as the giver of our liberty. The renegade asked her in Morisco whether her father was in the house. She replied that he was and that he was asleep.
"Then we will have to wake him and take him with us," said the renegade, "and everything of value in this fair house."

"No," said she, "my father must not on any account be touched, and there is nothing in the house except what I shall take, and that will be enough to enrich and satisfy all of you. Wait a little and you shall see." And with that she went in, telling us she would return immediately and asking us to keep quiet and not make any noise.

I asked the renegade what had passed between them, and when he told me, I declared that nothing should be done except in accordance with Zoraida's wishes. She now came back with a little trunk so full of gold crowns that she could barely carry it. Unfortunately her father woke up while this was going on, and hearing a noise in the garden came to the window. At once seeing that all those out there were Christians, he raised a tremendous outcry, calling out in Arabic, "Christians, Christians! Thieves, thieves!" — cries that threw us all into the greatest fear and confusion. But the renegade, seeing the danger we were in and how important it was for him to carry out his purpose before we were heard, rushed up to where Hadji Morato was, and some of our party went with him. I, however, did not dare to leave Zoraida, who had fallen almost fainting in my arms. To be brief, those who had gone upstairs acted so quickly that in an instant they came down carrying Hadji Morato with his hands bound and a napkin tied over his mouth to keep him from uttering a word, warning him at the same time that any attempt to speak would cost him his life. When his daughter caught sight of him she covered her eyes so as not to see him, and her father was horror-struck, not knowing how willingly she had placed herself in our hands. But now it was crucial for us to be on the move, and carefully and quickly we regained the vessel, where those who had remained on board were waiting in fear that some mishap had befallen us. It was barely two hours after nightfall when we were all on board the vessel, where the cords were removed from the hands of Zoraida's father, and the napkin from his mouth; but the renegade once more told him not to utter a word, or they would take his life. He, when he saw his daughter there, began to sigh piteously, and still more when he saw that I held her closely embraced and that she lay quiet, without resisting or complaining, or showing any reluctance; nevertheless he remained silent, lest they should carry out the repeated threats the renegade had made.

Finding herself now on board, and that we were about to push off with the oars, Zoraida, seeing her father there and the other Moors bound, asked the renegade to beg me as a favour to release the Moors and set her father at liberty, for she would rather drown herself in the sea than see a father who had loved her so dearly carried away captive before her eyes and on her account. The renegade repeated this to me, and I replied that I was very willing to do so; but he answered that it was not advisable, because if they were left there they would at once raise the country and stir up the city, and lead to the despatch of swift cruisers in pursuit, with us being taken by sea or land without any possibility of escape; and that the most that could be done was to set them free at the first Christian ground we reached. On this we all agreed; and Zoraida, when it was explained to her, along with the reasons that prevented us from doing what she wanted at once, was satisfied likewise. Then in glad silence and with cheerful eagerness each of our stout rowers took his oar, and commending ourselves to God with all our hearts, we began to shape our course for the island of Majorca, the nearest Christian land. However, with the Tramontana wind rising a little and the sea growing somewhat rough, it was impossible for us to keep a straight course for Majorca, and we were forced to coast in the direction of Oran — not without great unease, for fear we should be sighted from the town of Shershel, which lies on that coast not more than sixty miles from Algiers. We were also afraid of meeting on that course one of the galliots that usually come with goods from Tetuan; although each of us individually and all of us together felt confident that, if we met a merchant galliot (provided it was not a cruiser), not only would we not be lost, but we should take a vessel in which we could more safely make our voyage. As we pursued our course, Zoraida kept her head between my hands so as not to see her father, and I felt that she was praying to Lela Marien to help us.

We must have made about thirty miles when daybreak found us some three musket-shots off the land, which seemed to us deserted, without anyone to see us. For all that, however, by hard rowing we put a little farther out to sea, since it was now somewhat calmer; and having gained about two leagues, the word was given to row by batches while we ate something, for the vessel was well stocked. But the rowers said it was no time to take any rest: let food be served to those who were not rowing, but they would not leave their oars on any account. This was done. But now a stiff breeze began to blow, which obliged us to leave off rowing and make sail at once and steer for Oran, since it was impossible to keep any other course. All this was done very promptly, and under sail we ran more than eight miles an hour without any fear, except of coming across some vessel out on a raiding expedition. We gave the Moorish rowers some food, and the renegade comforted them by saying they were not being held captive, that we would set them free at the first opportunity.

The same was said to Zoraida's father, who replied, "Anything else, Christian, I might hope for or think likely from your generosity and good behaviour, but do not think me so simple as to imagine you will give me my liberty; for you would never have exposed yourselves to the danger of taking it from me only to restore it to me so generously, especially as you know who I am and the sum you can expect to receive for restoring it. If you will name that sum, I here offer you all you ask, for myself and for my unhappy daughter — or for her alone, since she is the greatest and most precious part of my soul."

As he said this he began to weep so bitterly that he filled us all with compassion and forced Zoraida to look at him. When she saw him weeping she was so moved that she rose from my feet and ran to throw her arms round him, and pressing her face to his they both gave way to such an outburst of tears that several of us were forced to keep them company.

But when her father saw her in full dress and with all her jewels on, he said to her in his own language, "What does this mean, my daughter? Last night, before this terrible misfortune that has fallen on us, I saw you in your everyday and indoor clothes; and now, without having had time to dress yourself, and without my bringing you any joyful news to occasion adorning and bedecking yourself, I see you arrayed in the finest attire it would be in my power to give you when fortune was kindest to us. Answer me this; it troubles and surprises me more than even this misfortune itself."

The renegade interpreted to us what the Moor said to his daughter; she, however, returned him no answer. But when he noticed in one corner of the vessel the little trunk in which she kept her jewels — which he knew very well he had left in Algiers and had not brought to the garden — he was still more amazed, and asked her how that trunk had come into our hands, and what was in it. To which the renegade, without waiting for Zoraida to reply, answered, "Do not trouble yourself by asking your daughter Zoraida so many questions, señor, for one answer I will give you will serve for all. I would have you know that she is a Christian, and that it is she who has been the file for our chains and our deliverer from captivity. She is here of her own free will, and as glad, I imagine, to find herself in this position as one who escapes from darkness into the light, from death to life, and from suffering to glory."
"Daughter, is this true, what he says?" cried the Moor.
"It is," replied Zoraida.
"That you are truly a Christian," said the old man, "and that you have given your father into the power of his enemies?"
To which Zoraida answered, "A Christian I am, but it is not I who have placed you in this position, for it was never my wish to leave you or do you harm, but only to do good to myself."
"And what good have you done yourself, daughter?" said he.
"Ask that," said she, "of Lela Marien, for she can tell you better than I can."

The Moor had hardly heard these words when with remarkable speed he flung himself headfirst into the sea, where no doubt he would have drowned had not the long and full robe he wore held him up for a little on the surface of the water. Zoraida cried out to us to save him, and we all hurried to help, and seizing him by his robe we drew him in half drowned and unconscious. Zoraida was so distressed that she wept over him as piteously and bitterly as if he were already dead. We turned him face down and he discharged a great quantity of water, and at the end of two hours he came to. Meanwhile, the wind having changed, we were forced to head for the land and ply our oars to avoid being driven on shore; but it was our good fortune to reach a creek on one side of a small promontory or cape called by the Moors that of the "Cava rumia," which in our language means "the wicked Christian woman." Their tradition is that La Cava — the woman through whom Spain was lost — lies buried at that spot; _cava_ in their language meaning "wicked woman," and _rumia_ "Christian." Moreover, they count it unlucky to anchor there when need compels them, and they never do so otherwise. For us, however, it was not the resting-place of the wicked woman but a haven of safety for our relief, so much had the sea now got up. We posted a lookout on shore, never let the oars out of our hands, ate of the stores the renegade had laid in, and implored God and Our Lady with all our hearts to help and protect us, so that we might bring to a happy ending so prosperous a beginning. At Zoraida's entreaty, orders were given to set on shore her father and the other Moors who were still bound, for she could not bear, nor could her tender heart endure, to see her father in bonds and her fellow-countrymen prisoners before her eyes. We promised her to do this at the moment of departure, since the place was uninhabited and we ran no risk in releasing them there.

Our prayers were not so far in vain as to go unheard by heaven, for after a while the wind changed in our favour, made the sea calm, and invited us once more to resume our voyage with good heart. Seeing this, we untied the Moors, and one by one put them ashore, at which they were filled with amazement. But when we came to land Zoraida's father, who had now completely recovered his senses, he said:

"Why do you suppose, Christians, that this wicked woman is glad you are giving me my liberty? Do you think it is because of the affection she bears me? No, indeed — it is only because of the hindrance my presence is to the carrying out of her base designs. And do not imagine that it is her belief that yours is better than ours that has led her to change her religion; it is only because she knows that immodesty is more freely practised in your country than in ours." Then turning to Zoraida, while I and another of the Christians held him fast by both arms in case he should do some mad act, he said to her, "Infamous girl, misguided maiden, where in your blindness and madness are you going, in the hands of these dogs, our natural enemies? Cursed be the hour I begot you! Cursed the luxury and indulgence in which I raised you!"

Seeing that he was not likely to stop any time soon, I hurried to put him on shore, and from there he kept up his curses and lamentations aloud, calling on Mohammed to pray Allah to destroy us, to confound us, to make an end of us. When, having set sail, we could no longer hear what he said, we could still see what he did — how he plucked out his beard and tore his hair and lay writhing on the ground. Once he raised his voice to such a pitch that we were able to hear what he said: "Come back, dear daughter, come back to shore; I forgive you everything. Let those men have the money — it is theirs now — and come back to comfort your sorrowing father, who will give up his life on this barren strand if you leave him."

All this Zoraida heard, and heard with sorrow and tears, and all she could say in answer was, "May Allah grant that Lela Marien, who has made me become a Christian, give you comfort in your sorrow, my father. Allah knows that I could not do otherwise than I have done, and that these Christians owe nothing to my will; for even had I wished not to go with them but to remain at home, it would have been impossible for me, so eagerly did my soul urge me on to the accomplishment of this purpose, which I feel to be as righteous as to you, dear father, it seems wicked."

But neither could her father hear her nor we see him when she said this. And so, while I consoled Zoraida, we turned our attention to our voyage, in which a breeze from the right point so favoured us that we made sure of finding ourselves off the coast of Spain by daybreak the next morning. But as good seldom or never comes pure and unmixed, without being followed by some disturbing evil that gives it a shock, our fortune — or perhaps the curses the Moor had hurled at his daughter, for whatever kind of father they come from these are always to be dreaded — brought it about that, when we were now in mid-sea about three hours into the night, running with all sail set and oars lashed (the favouring breeze saving us the trouble of using them), we saw by the light of the moon, which shone brilliantly, a square-rigged vessel in full sail close to us, luffing up and standing across our course, and so close that we had to strike sail to avoid running foul of her, while they too put the helm hard up to let us pass. They came to the side of the ship to ask who we were, where we were bound, and where we came from; but as they asked this in French our renegade said, "Let no one answer, for no doubt these are French corsairs who plunder all comers."

On this warning no one said a word; but after we had drawn a little ahead and the vessel was now lying to leeward, suddenly they fired two guns, apparently both loaded with chain-shot, for with one they cut our mast in half and brought it and the sail down into the sea, and the other, fired at the same moment, sent a ball into our vessel amidships, staving her in completely but without doing any further damage. We, however, finding ourselves sinking, began to shout for help and call on those in the ship to pick us up as we were beginning to fill. They then lay to, and lowering a skiff or boat, as many as a dozen Frenchmen, well armed with matchlocks and their matches burning, got into it and came alongside. Seeing how few we were, and that our vessel was going down, they took us in, telling us this had come to us through our incivility in not giving them an answer. Our renegade took the trunk containing Zoraida's wealth and dropped it into the sea without anyone noticing what he did. In short, we went on board with the Frenchmen, who, after finding out everything they wanted to know about us, rifled us of everything we had, as if they had been our bitterest enemies; and from Zoraida they took even the anklets she wore on her feet. But the distress they caused her did not distress me as much as the fear I was in that, after robbing her of her rich and precious jewels, they would go on to rob her of the most precious jewel of all, the one she valued more than any other. The desires of those people, however, do not go beyond money, but their greed for that is insatiable, and on this occasion was carried to such a pitch that they would have taken even the clothes we wore as captives if they had been worth anything to them. It was the advice of some of them to throw us all into the sea wrapped up in a sail, because they planned to trade at some of the ports of Spain, giving themselves out as Bretons, and if they brought us in alive they would be punished as soon as the robbery was discovered. But the captain (the one who had plundered my beloved Zoraida) said he was satisfied with the prize he had got, and that he would not touch at any Spanish port but pass the Straits of Gibraltar by night, or as best he could, and make for La Rochelle, from which he had sailed. So they agreed by common consent to give us the skiff belonging to their ship and everything we needed for the short voyage that remained to us; and they did so the next day on coming in sight of the Spanish coast — at which, with the joy we felt, all our sufferings and miseries were as completely forgotten as if they had never been endured, such is the delight of recovering lost liberty.

It may have been about midday when they put us in the boat, giving us two kegs of water and some biscuit. The captain, moved by I know not what compassion, as the lovely Zoraida was about to embark, gave her some forty gold crowns and would not let his men take from her the same garments she has on now. We got into the boat, returning them thanks for their kindness to us, and showing ourselves grateful rather than indignant. They stood out to sea, steering for the straits; we, looking to no compass other than the land in front of us, set to rowing with such energy that by sunset we were so near it that we thought we might easily land before the night was far advanced. But as the moon did not show that night, and the sky was clouded, and we did not know where we were, it did not seem prudent to make for the shore, as several of us advised, saying we ought to run ourselves ashore even if it were on rocks and far from any habitation, since this way we should be relieved from the anxiety we naturally felt of the prowling vessels of the Tetuan corsairs, who leave Barbary at nightfall and are on the Spanish coast by daybreak, where they commonly take some prize and then go home to sleep in their own houses. But of the conflicting counsels the one adopted was that we should approach gradually and land where we could if the sea was calm enough to permit it. This was done, and a little before midnight we drew near to the foot of a huge, lofty mountain, not so close to the sea that it did not leave a narrow space where we could land conveniently. We ran our boat up on the sand, all sprang out and kissed the ground, and with tears of joyful satisfaction returned thanks to God our Lord for all his incomparable goodness to us on our voyage. We took the provisions out of the boat, drew it up on the shore, and then climbed a long way up the mountain, for even there we could not feel easy in our hearts, nor persuade ourselves that it was Christian soil now under our feet.

The dawn came more slowly, I think, than we could have wished. We completed the ascent in order to see if from the summit any habitation or any shepherds' huts could be made out, but strain our eyes as we might, we could see neither dwelling nor human being, nor path nor road. We decided, however, to push on farther, since before long we must surely see someone who could tell us where we were. But what distressed me most was to see Zoraida going on foot over that rough ground; for though I once carried her on my shoulders, she was more wearied by my weariness than rested by the rest, and so she would never again let me undergo the exertion, and went on very patiently and cheerfully while I led her by the hand. We had gone rather less than a quarter of a league when the sound of a little bell fell on our ears, a clear proof that there were flocks nearby. Looking about carefully to see if any were within view, we saw a young shepherd quietly and unsuspectingly trimming a stick with his knife at the foot of a cork tree. We called to him, and he, raising his head, sprang nimbly to his feet — for, as we afterwards learned, the first people he saw were the renegade and Zoraida, and seeing them in Moorish dress he imagined that all the Moors of Barbary were upon him. Plunging into the thicket in front of him with remarkable speed, he began to raise a tremendous outcry, shouting, "The Moors — the Moors have landed! To arms, to arms!" We were all thrown into perplexity by these cries, not knowing what to do; but reflecting that the shepherd's shouts would raise the country and that the mounted coast-guard would come at once to see what was the matter, we agreed that the renegade must strip off his Turkish garments and put on a captive's jacket or coat, which one of our party gave him at once, though he himself was reduced to his shirt. And so, commending ourselves to God, we followed the same road we saw the shepherd take, expecting every moment that the coast-guard would be on us. Nor did our expectation deceive us, for two hours had not passed when, coming out of the brushwood into the open ground, we saw some fifty mounted men swiftly approaching at a hand-gallop. As soon as we saw them we stopped, waiting for them; but as they came close and, instead of the Moors they were after, saw a band of poor Christians, they were taken aback, and one of them asked if it could be we who were the reason the shepherd had raised the alarm. I said "Yes," and as I was about to explain to him what had happened, and where we came from and who we were, one of the Christians in our party recognised the horseman who had asked the question, and before I could say anything more he exclaimed:

"Thanks be to God, sirs, for bringing us to such good quarters! Unless I am much mistaken, the ground we stand on is that of Velez Malaga, unless all my years of captivity have made me unable to remember that you, señor, who ask who we are, are Pedro de Bustamante, my uncle."
The Christian captive had hardly uttered these words when the horseman threw himself off his horse and ran to embrace the young man, crying:

"Nephew of my soul and life! I recognise you now; and long have I mourned you as dead — I, and my sister, your mother, and all your kin still alive, whom God has been pleased to preserve so they may enjoy the happiness of seeing you. We knew long since that you were in Algiers, and from the look of your clothes and those of all this company, I conclude that you have had a miraculous restoration to liberty."
"It is true," replied the young man, "and by-and-by we will tell you everything."

As soon as the horsemen understood we were Christian captives, they dismounted, and each offered his horse to carry us to the city of Velez Malaga, a league and a half away. Some of them went to fetch the boat to the city, after we had told them where we had left it; others took us up behind them, and Zoraida was placed on the horse of the young man's uncle. The whole town came out to meet us, for by this time they had heard of our arrival from someone who had gone on ahead. They were not astonished to see liberated captives or captive Moors, since people on that coast are well used to seeing both; but they were astonished at the beauty of Zoraida, which was just then heightened both by the exertion of travelling and by joy at finding herself on Christian soil and relieved of all fear of being lost. This had brought such a glow to her face that — unless my affection for her was deceiving me — I would venture to say there was not a more beautiful creature in the world, at least none that I had ever seen. We went straight to the church to return thanks to God for the mercies we had received, and when Zoraida entered it she said there were faces there like Lela Marien's. We told her they were her images, and as well as he could the renegade explained to her what they meant, that she might adore them as if each of them were the very same Lela Marien who had spoken to her. Having great intelligence and a quick, clear instinct, she understood at once everything he said to her about them. From there they took us away and distributed us among different houses in the town; but as for the renegade, Zoraida, and myself, the Christian who had come with us brought us to the house of his parents, who had a fair share of the gifts of fortune and treated us with as much kindness as they did their own son.

We remained six days in Velez, at the end of which the renegade, having found out everything he needed to do, set out for the city of Granada to restore himself to the sacred bosom of the Church through the medium of the Holy Inquisition. The other freed captives took their leave, each going the way that seemed best to him; and Zoraida and I were left alone, with nothing more than the crowns the courtesy of the Frenchman had given Zoraida, with which I bought the beast she rides. Attending her for now as her father and squire rather than as her husband, we are now going to find out if my father is still living, or if any of my brothers has had better fortune than mine; though, since heaven has made me Zoraida's companion, I think no other lot, however happy, could be given to me that I would rather have. The patience with which she endures the hardships poverty brings with it, and the eagerness she shows to become a Christian, are such that they fill me with admiration and bind me to serve her all my life — though the happiness I feel in seeing myself hers, and her mine, is disturbed and marred by not knowing whether I shall find any corner to shelter her in my own country, or whether time and death may have made such changes in the fortunes and lives of my father and brothers that I shall hardly find anyone who knows me, if they are not alive.

I have no more of my story to tell you, gentlemen. Whether it has been an interesting or a curious one, let your better judgments decide; all I can say is that I would gladly have told it to you more briefly, although my fear of wearying you has made me leave out more than one detail.

title: Part 1, Chapter 42
paragraphs: Which deals with what else happened at the inn, and with several other things worth knowing

With these words the captive fell silent, and Don Fernando said to him, "Honestly, captain, the way you have told this remarkable adventure matched the novelty and strangeness of the material itself. The whole story is curious and out of the ordinary, full of incidents that leave the listeners amazed and astonished. We have taken such pleasure in hearing it that we would happily have you start it over again, even if tomorrow found us still caught up in the same tale." While he was saying this, Cardenio and the others offered to help him in any way within their power, in words so kind and sincere that the captain was deeply touched by their goodwill. Don Fernando in particular offered, if the captive would return with him, to arrange for his brother the marquis to stand as godfather at Zoraida's baptism, and to provide him personally with whatever he needed to return to his own region with the dignity and comfort he deserved. The captive thanked them all very courteously for this, but he would not accept any of their generous offers.

By now night had fallen, and as it did, a coach pulled up at the inn, escorted by several men on horseback who asked for lodging. The landlady answered that there wasn't a hand's breadth of space left unoccupied in the entire inn.
"Even so," said one of the men who had ridden up, "room will have to be found for his lordship the Judge here."

At that title the landlady grew flustered and said, "Señor, the truth is I have no beds; but if his lordship the Judge is carrying one with him, as he surely is, then let him come in and be welcome, because my husband and I will give up our own room to accommodate his worship."

"Very well, so be it," said the squire. By this time a man had stepped out of the coach whose clothing announced at a glance the office and position he held, since the long robe with ruffled sleeves he wore showed that he was, as his servant had said, a Judge of appeal. He was leading by the hand a young girl in traveling clothes, around sixteen years old, with such an aristocratic air, so beautiful and so graceful, that everyone was filled with admiration the moment she appeared. If they had not already seen Dorothea, Luscinda, and Zoraida, who were there in the inn, they would have believed that beauty like this girl's would be hard to find anywhere. Don Quixote was present when the Judge and the young lady came in, and the instant he saw him he said, "Your worship may enter this castle with confidence and make yourself at home; for though the lodgings are scant and poor, no quarters are so cramped or inconvenient that they cannot make room for arms and letters — above all when arms and letters have beauty as their guide and leader, as the letters your worship represents have in this lovely maiden. For her, not only should castles throw themselves open and surrender, but rocks should split apart and mountains divide and bow down to receive her. Enter, your worship, I say, into this paradise, for here you will find stars and suns to keep company with the heaven your worship brings with you; here you will find arms at their supreme excellence and beauty at its highest perfection."

The Judge was astonished by Don Quixote's language, and he studied him very carefully, no less amazed by his appearance than by his talk. Before he could find any words to answer, he got a fresh surprise when he saw Luscinda, Dorothea, and Zoraida standing across from him; having heard about the new guests and the young lady's beauty, they had come to see her and welcome her. Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the priest, however, greeted him in a more intelligible and polished manner. In short, the Judge made his entrance thoroughly bewildered, as much by what he saw as by what he heard, and the lovely ladies of the inn gave the lovely girl a warm welcome. On the whole he could tell that everyone present was a person of quality, but Don Quixote's figure, face, and bearing left him completely at a loss. Once all the courtesies had been exchanged and the inn's accommodations looked into, the earlier arrangement was confirmed: all the women would withdraw to the garret already mentioned, and the men would stay outside as if standing guard over them. The Judge was therefore quite happy to let his daughter — for that is who the girl was — go with the ladies, which she did very willingly; and with part of the innkeeper's narrow bed and half of what the Judge had brought with him, they settled themselves for the night more comfortably than they had expected.

The moment the captive saw the Judge his heart had leaped, somehow telling him that this was his brother, and he asked one of the accompanying servants what his name was and whether he knew what part of the country he came from. The servant replied that he was called Licentiate Juan Perez de Viedma, and that he had heard he came from a village in the mountains of Leon. From this information, and from what he had seen himself, he felt certain that this was his brother — the one who had taken up letters on their father's advice. Excited and overjoyed, he drew Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the priest aside and told them how things stood, assuring them that the Judge was his brother. The servant had also told him that the Judge was now headed for the Indies, having been appointed Judge of the Supreme Court of Mexico; and he had learned, too, that the young lady was his daughter, whose mother had died giving birth to her, and that he had become very rich through the dowry left to him along with the daughter. He asked their advice on how he should reveal himself — or how to find out in advance whether, once he revealed himself, his brother would be ashamed to see him so poor, or would receive him with an open heart.

"Leave it to me to find that out," said the priest. "Though there is no reason to assume, señor captain, that you won't be welcomed warmly, because the worth and good sense evident in your brother's bearing make it unlikely that he will turn out arrogant or unfeeling, or that he won't know how to weigh the accidents of fortune at their true value."
"Still," said the captain, "I would rather not reveal myself abruptly, but in some roundabout way."
"I've already told you," said the priest, "that I will handle it in a way that satisfies us all."
By now supper was ready, and they all sat down at the table — except the captive and the ladies, who ate by themselves in their own room. In the middle of supper the priest said:

"Señor Judge, in Constantinople, where I was a captive for several years, I had a comrade who bore your worship's name, and that same comrade was one of the finest soldiers and captains in the entire Spanish infantry; but he had as large a share of misfortune as he had of gallantry and courage."
"And what was the captain's name, señor?" asked the Judge.

"His name was Ruy Perez de Viedma," the priest replied, "and he was born in a village in the mountains of Leon. He mentioned something about his father and his brothers which, if it hadn't come from a man as truthful as he was, I would have written off as one of those fables old women tell around the fire in winter: he said his father had divided his property among his three sons and given them advice sounder than anything Cato ever offered. But I can tell you this much — his choice to go off to the wars turned out so well that through his gallant conduct and courage, with no help beyond his own merit, he rose within a few years to captain of infantry, well on his way and positioned to receive command of a corps before long. But Fortune turned against him; just where he might have expected her favor, he lost it, and his liberty with it, on that glorious day when so many others recovered theirs — the battle of Lepanto. I lost mine at the Goletta, and after a string of adventures we ended up comrades in Constantinople. From there he went to Algiers, where he met with one of the most extraordinary adventures that ever happened to anyone in the world."

The priest then went on to recount briefly his brother's adventure with Zoraida, and the Judge listened to all of it so attentively that he had never been so completely an audience in his life. The priest, however, only went as far as the point where the Frenchmen robbed the people in the boat, and the poverty and hardship in which his comrade and the beautiful Moorish woman were left. He said he had not been able to learn what became of them afterward — whether they had reached Spain, or had been carried off to France by the Frenchmen.

The captain stood a little off to one side, listening to everything the priest said and watching every movement his brother made. As soon as the Judge saw that the priest had finished his story, he heaved a deep sigh and said, his eyes brimming with tears, "Oh, señor, if you only knew what news you have just given me, and how deeply it strikes home — so deeply that I have to show it with these tears that spring from my eyes despite all my worldly wisdom and self-control! That brave captain you speak of is my eldest brother. Being bolder and more high-minded than my other brother or me, he chose the honorable and worthy profession of arms — one of the three careers our father proposed to us, just as your comrade mentioned in that tale you took for a fable. I followed the path of letters, in which God and my own efforts have raised me to the position you see me in now. My second brother is in Peru, so wealthy that with what he has sent to my father and to me he has fully repaid the share he took with him, and has even put into my father's hands the means to indulge his natural generosity; thanks to him I too was able to pursue my studies in a more fitting and respectable manner and so reach my present standing. My father is still alive, though dying of anxiety for news of his eldest son, and he prays to God without ceasing that death will not close his eyes until he has looked upon his son's. What surprises me about my brother is that a man with so much common sense should have neglected to send any word of himself, either in his troubles and sufferings or in his prosperity; for if our father or any of us had known his situation, he would not have needed to wait for that miracle of the reed to obtain his ransom. But what troubles me now is the uncertainty: did those Frenchmen set him free, or did they murder him to cover up the robbery? All of this will make me continue my journey not with the satisfaction I started it in, but in the deepest melancholy and sadness. Oh, dear brother! If only I knew where you are right now — I would hurry to find you and free you from your sufferings, even if it cost me suffering of my own! Oh, if only I could carry the news to our old father that you are alive, even if you were in the deepest dungeon of Barbary; his wealth, and my brother's, and mine would get you out of there! Oh, beautiful and generous Zoraida — if only I could repay your kindness to a brother! If only I could be present at the rebirth of your soul, and at the wedding that would bring us all such happiness!"

The Judge said all this and more, with such deep emotion at the news of his brother that everyone who heard him shared in it and showed their sympathy with his grief. The priest, seeing how well he had succeeded in carrying out his plan and the captain's wishes, had no desire to keep them in distress any longer, so he rose from the table, went into the room where Zoraida was, and took her by the hand, with Luscinda, Dorothea, and the Judge's daughter following behind her. The captain was waiting to see what the priest would do; the priest took him by the other hand and walked with both of them over to where the Judge and the other gentlemen were, and said, "Let your tears stop flowing, Señor Judge, and let your heart's desire be granted as fully as you could wish, for standing before you is your worthy brother and your good sister-in-law. The man you see here is Captain Viedma, and this is the beautiful Moorish woman who treated him so well. The Frenchmen I told you about have left them in the poverty you see — so that you can show the generosity of your kind heart."

The captain ran to embrace his brother, who placed both hands on his chest to get a good look at him, holding him at arm's length for a moment; but the instant he fully recognized him, he clasped him so tightly in his arms, shedding such tears of heartfelt joy, that most of those present could not help crying along with them. The words the brothers exchanged, the emotion they showed, can hardly be imagined, I suspect, much less set down in writing. They told each other briefly the events of their lives; they showed the true affection of brothers in all its strength. Then the Judge embraced Zoraida and put everything he owned at her disposal; then he had his daughter embrace her, and the lovely Christian and the beautiful Moorish woman drew fresh tears from every eye. And there stood Don Quixote, observing all these strange proceedings attentively without saying a word, attributing the whole thing to the chimeras of knight-errantry. They then agreed that the captain and Zoraida would return with his brother to Seville and send word to their father that he had been rescued and found, so that the old man could come and attend Zoraida's wedding and baptism; for it was impossible for the Judge to postpone his journey, since he had been informed that in a month's time the fleet would sail from Seville for New Spain, and missing the passage would have been a serious inconvenience for him. In short, everyone was pleased and delighted at the captive's good fortune; and since nearly two-thirds of the night was already gone, they decided to go to bed for what remained of it. Don Quixote offered to stand guard over the castle in case they were attacked by some giant or other malicious villain greedy for the great treasure of beauty the castle held. Those who knew him thanked him for this service, and they gave the Judge an account of his strange obsession, which amused him more than a little. Only Sancho Panza was fuming at how late they were getting to bed; and he, of all of them, made himself the most comfortable, stretching out on his donkey's harness and saddle-gear — which, as will be told later on, cost him dearly.

The ladies, then, had withdrawn to their room, and the others had settled themselves with as little discomfort as they could manage, while Don Quixote went outside the inn to act as sentinel of the castle, as he had promised. But it happened that a little before daybreak, a voice so musical and sweet reached the ladies' ears that it compelled them all to listen closely — especially Dorothea, who was lying awake with Doña Clara de Viedma (for that was the Judge's daughter's name) asleep at her side. No one could guess who was singing so sweetly, and the voice was not accompanied by any instrument. One moment it seemed to them that the singer was in the courtyard, the next moment in the stable; and while they were all listening intently, wondering, Cardenio came to the door and said, "Anyone who isn't asleep, listen — you'll hear a muleteer's voice that enchants as it chants."
"We're already listening to it, señor," said Dorothea. At that Cardenio went away, and Dorothea, giving the song her full attention, made out its words to be these:

title: Part 1, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Which tells the entertaining story of the mule driver, along with other strange things that happened at the inn
Poor me — I am Love's sailor, voyaging across Love's deep ocean; I don't know where the harbor lies, and I don't dare hope to reach it.
A single distant star is all I have to guide me — a brighter light than any of those old stars that Palinurus steered by.
I am carried along, drifting aimlessly, with no idea where it is taking me; I keep my gaze fixed on that star alone, blind to everything else around it.
But overcautious modesty, and a coldness both shy and cruel, act like clouds: just when I need it most, they deny me the light I long for.
Bright star, the goal of my yearning eyes as you shine above me — when you hide yourself from my sight, I will know that death is close to me.
The singer had gotten this far when it occurred to Dorothea that it wasn't fair for Clara to miss hearing such a sweet voice. So she shook her gently from side to side and woke her, saying:
"Forgive me for waking you, child, but I'm doing it so you can have the pleasure of hearing what may be the best voice you've ever heard in your whole life."

Clara woke up still drowsy and didn't understand at first what Dorothea was saying, so she asked her to repeat it. Dorothea did, and Clara immediately began to listen; but she had barely heard two lines as the singer went on when a strange trembling seized her, as if she were suffering a violent attack of quartan fever, and throwing her arms around Dorothea she said:

"Oh, dear lady of my soul and my life! Why did you wake me? The greatest kindness fortune could do me right now would be to close my eyes and ears so that I could neither see nor hear that unhappy musician."
"What are you talking about, child?" said Dorothea. "Why, they say this singer is a mule driver!"
"No — he is the lord of many estates," Clara replied, "and the one place he holds so firmly, in my heart, will never be taken from him unless he chooses to surrender it himself."
Dorothea was astonished at the girl's passionate language, which seemed far beyond whatever experience of life her tender age could possibly have given her, and so she said to her:

"You're speaking in a way I can't understand, Señora Clara. Explain yourself more clearly, and tell me what you mean by all this talk of hearts and estates and this musician whose voice has moved you so much. But don't tell me anything just yet — I don't want to lose the pleasure of listening to the singer by giving my attention to your outbursts, because I can hear he's beginning a new song with a new melody."

"Let him sing, in Heaven's name," Clara answered; and so as not to hear him she covered both ears with her hands, which surprised Dorothea all over again. But when she turned her attention back to the song, she found it went like this:
Sweet Hope, my support, you press on toward the goal you intend, making your own way forward, ignoring every hindrance and obstacle — have no fear if at every step you find that death is near.
The faint heart knows no victory, no joy of triumph; unblessed is the man who doesn't dare show Fortune a bold face, but instead surrenders soul and senses into the bondage of idleness.
If Love sells his goods at a high price, who can dispute his right to do it? What gold compares with anything that carries his stamp? And everyone knows that whatever costs little, we value cheaply.
A resolute love does not know the word "impossibility"; and though I can see my suit beset by endless obstacles, no despair will keep me bound to earth while heaven is there.

Here the voice stopped and Clara's sobbing started up again, all of which sharpened Dorothea's curiosity to know what could be the cause of such sweet singing and such bitter weeping. So she asked her once more what she had been about to say earlier. At this Clara, afraid that Luscinda might overhear her, wrapped her arms tightly around Dorothea and put her mouth so close to her ear that she could speak without any fear of being heard by anyone else, and said:

"This singer, dear señora, is the son of a gentleman from Aragon, the lord of two villages, who lives across from my father's house in Madrid. And although my father kept curtains over the windows of his house in winter and lattice screens in summer, somehow — I don't know how — this gentleman, who was a student at the time, saw me, whether at church or somewhere else I can't say. The truth is, he fell in love with me and let me know it from the windows of his house with so many signs and so many tears that I had to believe him, and even to love him, without knowing what it was he wanted from me. One of the signs he used to make was to link one hand in the other, telling me he wanted to marry me; and although I would have been glad if that could happen, being alone and motherless I didn't know who to confide in, so I left things as they were and showed him no favor — except, when my father and his were both away from home, raising the curtain or the lattice a little and letting him see me plainly, at which he would show such delight that he seemed about to go mad. Meanwhile the time for my father's departure arrived, and the young man learned of it, though not from me, since I never had the chance to tell him. He fell sick — from grief, I believe — and so on the day we left I couldn't see him to say goodbye, even if only with my eyes. But after we had been two days on the road, as we entered the posada of a village a day's journey from here, I saw him at the inn door dressed as a mule driver, and so well disguised that if I didn't carry his image engraved on my heart, it would have been impossible for me to recognize him. But I knew him, and I was amazed, and overjoyed. He watches me without my father suspecting anything — he always hides from him when he crosses my path on the road or at the posadas where we stop. And since I know who he is, and realize that for love of me he is making this whole journey on foot, through all this hardship, I could die of sorrow; wherever he sets his foot, I set my eyes. I don't know what he intends by coming, or how he managed to get away from his father, who loves him beyond all measure, both because he has no other heir and because the young man deserves it — as you'll see for yourself when you meet him. And I can tell you something more: everything he sings comes out of his own head, for I've heard people say he is a great scholar and a poet. What's more, every time I see him or hear him sing, I tremble all over, terrified that my father will recognize him and discover our feelings for each other. I have never spoken a single word to him in my life, and even so I love him so much that I couldn't live without him. That, dear señora, is everything I have to tell you about the musician whose voice has delighted you so much; from that alone you can easily see he is no mule driver, but a lord of hearts and of towns, as I told you already."

"Say no more, Doña Clara," said Dorothea at this, kissing her a thousand times over as she spoke. "Say no more, I tell you, and wait until daylight comes; then, trusting in God, I hope to manage this affair of yours so that it has the happy ending such an innocent beginning deserves."

"Oh, señora," said Doña Clara, "what ending can I hope for, when his father is of such high rank and so wealthy that he would think I wasn't fit to be even a servant to his son, much less his wife? And as for marrying without my father's knowledge — I wouldn't do it for anything in the world. All I want is for this young man to turn back and leave me; maybe by not seeing him, and with the long distance we still have to travel, this pain I'm feeling now will grow easier — though I admit the remedy I'm proposing will probably do me very little good. I don't know how the devil this happened, or how this love I have for him ever got in; I'm such a young girl, and he's barely more than a boy. Honestly, I believe we're both the same age, and I'm not even sixteen yet — my father says I'll turn sixteen on Michaelmas Day."

Dorothea couldn't help laughing at how much like a child Doña Clara sounded. "Let's sleep now, señora," she said, "for the little of the night that I suspect is left to us. God will soon send us daylight, and then we'll set everything right, or I'll know the reason why."

With that they fell asleep, and deep silence settled over the whole inn. The only people still awake were the landlady's daughter and her servant Maritornes, who, knowing Don Quixote's particular weakness, and that he was outside the inn standing guard in armor and on horseback, decided between the two of them to play some trick on him, or at the very least to amuse themselves for a while by listening to his nonsense. As it happened, there was not a single window in the whole inn that faced outward except a hole in the wall of a straw loft, through which they used to throw out the straw. The two semi-damsels stationed themselves at this hole and watched Don Quixote on his horse, leaning on his pike and heaving, every so often, sighs so deep and mournful that each one seemed to tear his soul up by the roots. And they could hear him, too, saying in a soft, tender, loving voice, "Oh my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, perfection of all beauty, summit and crown of intelligence, treasure house of grace, storehouse of virtue, and, in short, the ideal of everything good, honorable, and delightful in this world! What is your grace doing right now? Could you, by any chance, be thinking of your enslaved knight, who of his own free will has exposed himself to such great dangers, and all to serve you? Bring me news of her, oh luminary of the three faces! Perhaps at this very moment, envious of hers, you are gazing at her as she paces back and forth along some gallery of her sumptuous palaces, or leans over some balcony, considering how — while preserving her purity and her greatness — she might ease the torment this wretched heart of mine endures for her sake; what glory should reward my sufferings, what rest my labors, and finally what death my life, and what payment my services. And you, oh sun, who are doubtless even now hurrying to harness your horses so you can rise early and come out to see my lady — when you see her, I beg you to greet her on my behalf. But take care, when you see her and greet her, not to kiss her face; for I will be more jealous of you than you were of that swift-footed ingrate who made you sweat and run so hard across the plains of Thessaly, or along the banks of the Peneus — I don't remember exactly where it was you ran on that occasion — in your jealousy and your love."
Don Quixote had gotten this far in his pitiful speech when the landlady's daughter began signaling to him, calling, "Señor, come over here, please."

At these signals and the sound of the voice, Don Quixote turned his head and saw, by the light of the moon, which was then shining at its fullest, that someone was calling to him from the hole in the wall — which to him looked like a window, and what's more, one with a gilded grating, the kind that grand castles, such as he believed the inn to be, ought to have. And it instantly occurred to his imagination that, as on the previous occasion, the lovely maiden, the daughter of the lady of the castle, overcome with love for him, had come back to try to win his affections. With that idea in mind, and not wanting to seem discourteous or ungrateful, he turned Rocinante's head and approached the hole, and when he saw the two wenches he said:

"I pity you, beautiful lady, for having directed your loving thoughts toward a place from which it is impossible for you to receive the response your great merit and noble birth deserve. But you must not blame this unhappy knight-errant for it, since love has made him incapable of giving himself to any woman except the one he made the absolute mistress of his soul the very first moment his eyes fell on her. Forgive me, noble lady, and withdraw to your chamber, and do not, by declaring your passion any further, force me to show myself even more ungrateful. And if, out of the love you bear me, you should find there is anything else within my power that could satisfy you — anything except love itself — ask it of me; for I swear to you, by that sweet absent enemy of mine, to grant it this very instant, even if you should demand a lock of Medusa's hair, which was made entirely of snakes, or even the very rays of the sun sealed up in a glass vial."
"My mistress wants nothing of that kind, sir knight," Maritornes said at this point.
"Then what is it, discreet lady, that your mistress does want?" Don Quixote replied.

"Just one of your fair hands," said Maritornes, "so she can pour out over it the great passion that has brought her to this opening at such risk to her honor; because if her lord father had heard her, the smallest piece he would slice off her would be her ear."

"I'd like to see him try that," said Don Quixote. "But he had better watch himself, unless he wants to meet the most disastrous end any father in the world ever met for laying hands on the tender limbs of a lovestruck daughter."

Maritornes felt certain that Don Quixote would offer the hand she had asked for, and having made up her mind what to do, she climbed down from the hole and went into the stable, where she took the halter of Sancho Panza's donkey, and hurried back to the hole just as Don Quixote had planted himself standing on Rocinante's saddle so that he could reach the grated window where he imagined the lovesick maiden to be. Holding out his hand to her, he said, "Lady, take this hand — or rather, this scourge of the evildoers of the earth. Take, I say, this hand, which no other woman's hand has ever touched, not even hers who has complete possession of my entire body. I give it to you not so that you may kiss it, but so that you may study the structure of its sinews, the tight network of its muscles, the breadth and capacity of its veins, and from all that deduce how strong the arm must be that has such a hand."

"We'll see about that soon enough," said Maritornes; and making a slip-knot in the halter, she looped it over his wrist, climbed down from the hole, and tied the other end very firmly to the bolt of the straw-loft door.

Feeling the roughness of the rope on his wrist, Don Quixote exclaimed, "Your grace seems to be grating my hand rather than caressing it. Don't treat it so harshly — it is not to blame for the offense my resolve has given you, and it isn't fair to take out all your vengeance on so small a part. Remember that a woman who loves so well should not take her revenge so cruelly."

But there was no one left now to hear these words of Don Quixote's, because the moment Maritornes had tied him, she and the other girl ran off, nearly dying of laughter, leaving him tethered in such a way that it was impossible for him to free himself.

He was, as we have said, standing on Rocinante, with his arm pushed through the hole and his wrist tied to the bolt of the door, in tremendous fear and dread of being left hanging by the arm if Rocinante shifted one way or the other; so he didn't dare make the slightest movement, although given Rocinante's patience and placid temperament he had good reason to expect the horse would stand without budging for a full century. Finding himself stuck fast, then, and the ladies gone, he began to imagine that all this had been done by enchantment, as on the previous occasion when, in this same castle, that enchanted Moor of a carrier had given him such a beating; and in his heart he cursed his own lack of sense and judgment in daring to enter the castle a second time after coming off so badly the first — it being a settled rule among knights-errant that when they have attempted an adventure and failed at it, this is a sign that it is reserved not for them but for others, and that they therefore have no need to attempt it again. Even so, he pulled on his arm to see whether he could free himself, but it had been tied so securely that all his efforts were useless. True, he pulled gently, so that Rocinante wouldn't move; but however much he wanted to sit back down in the saddle, he had no choice except to stand upright or wrench his hand off. Then it was that he wished for the sword of Amadis, against which no enchantment of any kind had power; then he cursed his bad luck; then he dwelt on the loss the world would suffer from his absence while he remained there enchanted — for he believed, beyond all doubt, that enchanted he was; then he fell once more to thinking of his beloved Dulcinea del Toboso; then he called out to his good squire Sancho Panza, who, buried in sleep and stretched out on his donkey's packsaddle, was at that moment oblivious even of the mother who bore him; then he called on the sages Lirgandeo and Alquife to come to his aid; then he appealed to his good friend Urganda to rescue him; and finally morning found him in such despair and confusion that he was bellowing like a bull, for he had no hope that daylight would bring any relief to his suffering, which he believed would last forever, since he was enchanted. He was convinced of this by seeing that Rocinante never stirred, much or little; and he felt sure that he and his horse were to remain in that state, without eating or drinking or sleeping, until the evil influence of the stars had passed, or until some other, wiser enchanter broke the spell.

But in this conclusion he was badly mistaken, for day had barely begun to break when four men on horseback rode up to the inn, well equipped and well outfitted, with flintlock muskets slung across their saddlebows. They shouted and pounded loudly at the gate of the inn, which was still shut; and seeing this, Don Quixote, even from where he was, did not forget his duty as sentinel, and called out in a loud, imperious voice, "Knights, or squires, or whatever you may be — you have no right to knock at the gates of this castle. It is obvious enough that those inside are either asleep, or else are not in the habit of opening the fortress until the sun's rays have spread over the whole face of the earth. Withdraw to a distance and wait until it is broad daylight, and then we shall see whether it is proper to open to you or not."

"What the devil kind of fortress or castle is this," said one of them, "that we have to stand on such ceremony? If you're the innkeeper, tell them to open up for us. We're travelers who only want to feed our horses and move on — we're in a hurry."
"Do I look to you like an innkeeper, gentlemen?" said Don Quixote.
"I don't know what you look like," the other answered, "but I do know that you're talking nonsense when you call this inn a castle."

"A castle it is," Don Quixote returned, "and more than that — one of the finest in this whole province. And inside it are people who have held the scepter in their hand and worn the crown on their head."

"It would be better the other way around," said the traveler — "the scepter on the head and the crown in the hand. But if that's the case, maybe there's a company of actors staying inside; for them it's an everyday thing to have those crowns and scepters you're talking about. Because in an inn as small as this one, and where everyone keeps so quiet, I can't believe anyone genuinely entitled to crowns and scepters would have taken lodging."
"You know very little of the world," Don Quixote replied, "if you are ignorant of things that happen all the time in knight-errantry."

But the spokesman's companions, growing tired of this exchange with Don Quixote, went back to pounding on the gate with such fury that the innkeeper woke up — and not only he, but everyone else in the inn — and he got up to ask who was knocking. At that moment it happened that one of the horses belonging to the four men seeking entry went over to sniff at Rocinante, who, melancholy, dejected, and with drooping ears, stood motionless, holding up his sorely stretched master; and since he was, after all, made of flesh, though he looked as if he were carved from wood, he couldn't help responding and sniffing back at the one who had come to pay him these attentions. But he had barely moved at all when Don Quixote lost his footing; and slipping off the saddle, he would have crashed to the ground had he not been left hanging by the arm — which caused him such agony that he believed his wrist was being sliced through or his arm torn from its socket. He hung so close to the ground that he could just touch it with his feet, which only made things worse for him; for, feeling how little he needed to be able to plant his feet flat, he strained and stretched as hard as he could to get a foothold — exactly like victims of the strappado torture, set at "touch and no touch," who increase their own suffering by their violent efforts to stretch themselves, deceived by the hope that with just a little more effort they will reach the ground.

title: Part 1, Chapter 44
paragraphs: In which the extraordinary adventures at the inn continue

Don Quixote was shouting so loudly, in fact, that the landlord threw open the gate of the inn in a hurry and came out alarmed, running to see who was making such a racket, and the people outside joined him. Maritornes, who had been woken by the same uproar and guessed what was going on, ran up to the loft and, without anyone noticing her, untied the halter that Don Quixote was hanging from. Down he dropped to the ground in full view of the landlord and the travelers, who came up and asked him what was wrong with him that he was yelling like that. Without answering a word, he pulled the rope off his wrist, got to his feet, leaped onto Rocinante, braced his shield on his arm, set his lance in position, and after riding a wide circuit around the plain came back at a half-gallop, declaring:
"Whoever claims that I was enchanted with good reason — provided my lady the Princess Micomicona gives me permission to do so — I call him a liar, I challenge him, and I defy him to single combat."

The newly arrived travelers were astonished at Don Quixote's words, but the landlord cleared up their confusion by telling them who he was and saying they shouldn't pay him any attention, since he was out of his mind. They then asked the landlord whether by any chance a boy of about fifteen had come to the inn, dressed like a mule driver and looking such and such a way — and the description they gave was of Doña Clara's lover. The landlord answered that there were so many people at the inn that he hadn't noticed the person they were asking about. But one of them, spotting the coach the Judge had arrived in, said, "He's here, no question — this is the coach he's been following. Let one of us stay at the gate and the rest go in to look for him. Actually, it would be a good idea for one of us to circle around the inn too, in case he tries to escape over the wall of the yard." "Agreed," said another; and while two of them went inside, one stayed at the gate and the other walked the perimeter of the inn. The landlord watched all this, unable to figure out why they were taking so many precautions, though he understood they were looking for the boy they had described to him.

By now it was broad daylight, and for that reason — and because of the noise Don Quixote had made — everyone was awake and up, especially Doña Clara and Dorothea, who had both slept badly that night: one out of agitation at having her lover so close, the other out of curiosity to see him. When Don Quixote saw that none of the four travelers paid him any attention or answered his challenge, he was furious — ready to die of indignation and rage. If he could have found anything in the rules of chivalry making it lawful for a knight-errant to take on or get involved in a new enterprise after he had pledged his word and faith not to commit himself to any until he had finished the one he was already bound to, he would have attacked the whole lot of them and forced them to answer whether they liked it or not. But considering that it would not be proper, or right, to begin any new venture until he had restored Micomicona to her kingdom, he had to hold his tongue and wait quietly to see how the travelers' business would play out. One of them found the boy they were looking for, sleeping beside a mule driver, with no idea that anyone was coming after him, much less that he would be found.
The man grabbed him by the arm and said, "This outfit really suits you, Señor Don Luis — and the bed I find you in certainly matches the luxury your mother raised you in."

The boy rubbed his sleepy eyes and stared for a moment at the man holding him, then recognized him as one of his father's servants. The shock left him so stunned that for a while he couldn't find a word to say, while the servant went on: "There's nothing for it now, Señor Don Luis, but to come quietly and go back home — unless you want my lord, your father, to depart for the next world, because nothing else can come of the grief your absence is causing him."
"But how did my father know I had taken this road, and in these clothes?" said Don Luis.

"It was a student you confided your plans to," the servant answered, "who revealed them, moved by pity at the distress he saw your father suffering when you went missing. So your father sent four of his servants out to find you, and here we all are at your service — happier than you can imagine that we'll be back so soon and able to return you to the eyes that long for you so much."
"That will be as I choose, or as heaven decides," Don Luis replied.
"What can you choose, or heaven decide," said the other, "except to agree to come back? Anything else is impossible."

The whole exchange between the two of them was overheard by the mule driver lying next to Don Luis, who got up and went to report what had happened to Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the others, who by now had gotten dressed. He told them how the man had addressed the boy as "Don," what words had passed between them, and how the man wanted him to go back to his father, which the boy refused to do. With this, and with what they already knew of the remarkable voice heaven had given him, they all became very eager to learn more precisely who he was — and even to help him if anyone tried to use force against him. So they hurried over to where he was still talking and arguing with his servant. At that moment Dorothea came out of her room with Doña Clara trembling behind her; calling Cardenio aside, she briefly told him the story of the singer and Doña Clara, while he in turn told her what had just happened — how his father's servants had come looking for him. But he didn't speak quietly enough, and Doña Clara overheard, which upset her so badly that if Dorothea hadn't rushed to hold her up, she would have collapsed to the ground. Cardenio then told Dorothea to take her back to her room, saying he would try to sort the whole thing out, and they did as he asked. By now all four men who had come after Don Luis were inside the inn and had surrounded him, pressing him to come back and console his father immediately, without a moment's delay. He answered that he could not possibly do so until he had settled a matter on which his life, his honor, and his heart all depended. The servants kept pressing him, insisting that they would absolutely not go back without him and that they would take him away whether he liked it or not.
"You will not do that," Don Luis replied, "unless you take me dead — though however you take me, it will be without life."

By this point the argument had drawn most of the people at the inn, especially Cardenio, Don Fernando, his companions, the Judge, the priest, the barber, and Don Quixote — who had decided there was no longer any need to stand guard over the castle. Cardenio, who already knew the young man's story, asked the men who wanted to take him away what their purpose was in trying to carry the boy off against his will.
